articles.body_text:
WWE NXT women's champion Kelani Jordan talks to OutKick about her title win at Heatwave, her match against Kendal Grey and more.

For at least one night, WWE’s Saturday Night’s Main Event will transform into Sunday Night’s Main Event as the showcase will take place in Atlanta on Labor Day weekend.

There are only four matches on the card, but each comes with heightened stakes.

Sunday Night’s Main Event is also set to feature a live performance from hip-hop artist Quavo, who will debut an unreleased track from his forthcoming album "QROMELIFE."

COMPLETE PRO WRESTLING COVERAGE ON OUTKICK

Read below for the match card and predictions on what will happen at the State Farm Arena on Sunday night. The event begins at 8 p.m. ET and can be seen on Peacock.

Tatum Paxley makes her entrance with Alexa Bliss and Charlotte Flair during SmackDown at Canadian Tire Centre in Ottawa, Ontario, on Aug. 28, 2026. (WWE via Getty Images)

A six-woman tag team match will take place to add to the longstanding feud among Charlotte Flair, Alexa Bliss and Tatum Paxley and Jade Cargill, Michin and B-Fab. It feels as though these women have been battling for months. Paxley was added to the fray when she made her SmackDown debut to back up Flair and Bliss. But Cargill, Michin and B-Fab have continuously been scrapping with Flair, Bliss and Paxley with Cargill and Flair seemingly fighting for the top contender spot to Chelsea Green’s women’s title.

Prediction: Flair, Bliss and Paxley put away Cargill, Michin and B-Fab.

Lil Yachty faces Baron Corbin during SmackDown at TD Garden in Boston, Mass., on Aug. 14, 2026. (WWE via Getty Images)

Baron Corbin returned to WWE and made an immediate impact. He earned a United States Championship shot at SummerSlam and defeated Trick Williams to win the title. Williams has been clawing his way back to the top, eyeing a title return. But he hasn’t been the only who has messed with Corbin. Lil Yachty, Williams’ valet, has kept nipping at Corbin’s heels. He’ll have a chance to help Williams in his match against Corbin. If Lil Yachty lasts at least five minutes in the ring with Corbin, Williams will get a rematch for the U.S. title. Expect some kind of shenanigans to take place in this match.

Prediction: Lil Yachty holds out for as long as he can against Corbin

Randy Orton and Cody Rhodes speak during SmackDown at Canadian Tire Centre in Ottawa, Ontario, on Aug. 28, 2026. (WWE via Getty Images)

It’s the long-awaited grudge match between WWE superstars Cody Rhodes and Randy Orton. Rhodes owes Orton another lick after getting punted in the head following their WrestleMania 42 Night 1 main event brawl. Rhodes won that match to retain the Undisputed WWE Championship. Orton got the last word with the kick that left Rhodes’ eye swollen. Since Orton’s return, the two have brawled constantly. Rhodes even went for a kill shot at one point. It caused SmackDown GM Nick Aldis to tell them if they continued to fight each other, they would never get a shot at a WWE championship again. It led to some harsh words from Orton, trying to coax Rhodes into hitting him. It didn’t work, but you could feel the tension between the two men building. This match will turn into a good ol’ fashioned slobber knocker.

Prediction: Cody Rhodes comes out on top in this one.

Bron Breakker and Oba Femi face off during Monday Night Raw at KeyBank Center in Buffalo, N.Y., on Aug. 17, 2026. (WWE via Getty Images)

There’s no tangible title on the line in this one – there’s only perception. Who is the future of WWE? Bron Breakker has been inside his own head for weeks as he grappled with Oba Femi’s rise in WWE. Breakker was on the mend as Femi defeated Brock Lesnar at WrestleMania 42, won the King of the Ring Tournament and seemingly ended Lesnar’s career at SummerSlam. Breakker failed to dispatch Seth Rollins and only became a tag team champion after Logan Paul got hurt. Breakker has shown that he still has that dog in him but Femi’s rule over the Raw roster has been cataclysmic for his opponents. Both men could very well be champions in the future, but for now, they fight to be the face of what is to come down the road.

Prediction: Breakker needs a win here to go back to the days in which he was considered the man with the loudest bark and the biggest bite. Breakker wins in what might be an upset.

Ryan Gaydos is a senior editor for Fox News Digital.

articles.title: How significant are the Yemeni government’s military gains against Houthis?
articles.excerpt:
Yemen’s internationally recognised government says its forces have made significant gains against the Houthis as fighting has escalated in recent weeks, raising fears of a return to full-scale war.

T...
articles.body_text:
Yemen’s internationally recognised government says its forces have made significant gains against the Houthis as fighting has escalated in recent weeks, raising fears of a return to full-scale war.

The government forces on Saturday said they had recaptured strategically located territory in Hodeidah province under Houthi control and advanced in western Taiz.

However, the latest gains do not yet amount to a decisive shift in Yemen’s long-running war.

The Iran-aligned Houthis still control the capital, Sanaa, and several other cities, and have themselves recently advanced around Taiz as they seek to threaten the government-held port of al-Makha (Mocha) and move towards areas bordering the strategically vital Bab al-Mandeb strait, the chokepoint that connects the Red Sea to the Arabian Sea.

The fighting comes amid a wider regional conflict involving Saudi Arabia, which is a key backer of the Yemeni government.

Riyadh has carried out air strikes against positions recently captured by the Houthis, as the battle increasingly focuses on territory leading towards one of the world’s most important shipping routes.

The government forces have been fighting the Houthis across several fronts, with some of the heaviest clashes in Taiz and Hodeidah provinces, and along the western Red Sea coast.

The SABA news agency, controlled by Yemen’s internationally recognised government, reported on Saturday that the Yemeni military had taken control of Hais district in Hodeidah, citing an unidentified military source.

Hais is strategically located at the junction of Hodeidah, Taiz and Ibb provinces. The Houthis have yet to comment on this latest development.

The source also said government forces have regained areas around the al-Barh junction in western Taiz and advanced towards Houthi positions. Taiz is divided between the Houthis and the Saudi-backed Yemeni government.

Fayad al-Numan, a Yemeni Information Ministry official, said government forces had also captured dozens of Houthi fighters during clashes in al-Jarahi district in southern Hodeidah.

Clashes in Taiz killed more than 60 people, including civilians, on Saturday, the AFP news agency reported.

On Thursday, fighting erupted as Houthi forces launched a major offensive along front lines in western Taiz and southern Hodeidah, using ballistic missiles, drones and artillery as ground forces attempted to advance towards government-held territory along the Red Sea coast.

The United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) said that about 1,800 families have been displaced over the past two days as fighting escalated in Taiz.

Fighting renewed in early August after months of calm when Yemeni government forces launched attacks on Houthi positions across multiple front lines.

The Yemeni government re-established control over major southern and eastern territories following a Saudi-backed counteroffensive and the subsequent dissolution of the UAE-backed Southern Transitional Council (STC) in January.

They now aim to unite Yemen after bringing the areas under Houthi control under one administration.

But the Houthis have pushed towards government-held areas near al-Makha and territory bordering the Bab al-Mandeb strait amid reinforcements and counteroffensives from the government forces.

The latest escalation follows a period of relative calm in Yemen that had largely held since a UN-brokered truce in April 2022. The ceasefire brought an end to major fighting since the Houthis’ capture of much of the country, including Sanaa, in 2014.

But Thursday’s attacks hint at a return to large-scale conflict.

The capture of Hais could be significant because of its position linking Hodeidah, Taiz and Ibb, while advances around al-Barh could help government forces push back against Houthi forces in western Taiz.

Presidential Leadership Council chairman Rashad al-Alimi said Yemen’s armed forces were capable of restoring control over the entire country and warned that Houthi “miscalculations” would lead to their “complete collapse”.

However, it is too early to describe the developments as a significant shift in control.

The Houthis had themselves seized positions near Taiz shortly before the government counteroffensive, according to an AFP news agency citing a military officer.

Houthi forces have also been attempting to cut off the government-held port of al-Makha, and advance towards areas bordering the Bab al-Mandeb strait.

The scale of government losses also shows how contested the battlefield remains. Twenty-six government soldiers were killed in several hours of fighting on Saturday alone, according to AFP’s military sources.

The escalation is also increasingly intertwined with the wider regional conflict linked to the US-Israel war on Iran.

The Iran-backed Houthis announced a maritime blockade of Saudi Arabia in July and began targeting Saudi ships and territory, while Saudi Arabia has carried out air strikes against Houthi positions in Taiz.

Bab al-Mandeb has become particularly important after Iran closed the Strait of Hormuz to commercial shipping. The Hormuz blockade has triggered a global energy crisis and is pushing the global economy into turbulence.

The waterway is a key transit route for Saudi oil, one of only two exit-entry points to the Red Sea, the other being the Suez Canal, raising the stakes as Houthi forces attempt to advance towards areas bordering the strait.

In July, Saudi Arabia announced a mission to form an international alliance to guard the Red Sea from attacks on shipping by Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen.

articles.title: No bailouts for Jaguar Land Rover amid reports of thousands of job cuts, says minister
articles.excerpt:
Carmaker, which is battling Trump tariffs and Chinese competitors, faces talks with union leaders and government

The government has signalled that it will not invest taxpayers’ money to limit job los...
articles.body_text:
Carmaker, which is battling Trump tariffs and Chinese competitors, faces talks with union leaders and government

The government has signalled that it will not invest taxpayers’ money to limit job losses at Jaguar Land Rover (JLR), after it emerged that the UK’s biggest carmaker is planning up to 4,000 redundancies.

Before crunch talks on Tuesday between JLR, union leaders and government officials, the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, said it was not his job to “intervene and run businesses”.

JLR, owned by the Indian conglomerate Tata Motors, told staff on Friday to expect a voluntary redundancy programme, as it tries to shore itself up against tough conditions with £1.7bn in cuts over two years.

The Coventry-based company is expected to provide further details on job cuts as soon as Monday, which could include an admission that compulsory job losses are possible.

The expected cuts, which represent almost 12% of JLR’s 34,000-strong UK workforce, threaten to provide an early reality check on Andy Burnham’s pledge to “reindustrialise” Britain.

Sources said they expect the redundancies, first reported in the Sunday Times, to be weighted towards more senior roles in management and research and development rather than shop floor production workers.

JLR is understood to be responding to pressure from Tata to offset a slump in sales, exacerbated by the fallout from last year’s cyber-attack and the impact of Donald Trump’s tariff wars.

Speaking on the BBC’s Laura Kuenssberg show on Sunday, Reynolds signalled that the government was unwilling to put money into the business to limit job losses.

Asked if there could be financial support to protect the jobs, he said: “Not if it’s to bail people out.

“If this is about making sure over time that workforce is right to make the business as ⁠competitive as possible, that’s the conversation we need to have,” Reynolds said, referring to the wider “challenging” environment for the auto sector.

“We need to adapt to evolving global market conditions,” a spokesperson for JLR, which has its largest plant in Solihull in the West Midlands, said.

Reynolds is expected to come under pressure to help staunch the number of job cuts from the Unite general secretary, Sharon Graham, during crunch talks with the JLR chief executive, PB Balaji, scheduled for Tuesday. Union officials will push for JLR to swerve compulsory job losses in favour of retraining or voluntary redundancy where possible.

While Reynolds indicated that no bailout would be available, he hinted at other options to support carmakers.

He refused to rule out watering down government targets for UK automakers to reach 80% zero-emission car sales by 2030, which would lead to a ban on the sale of new petrol and diesel cars by 2035, pointing to an open consultation on the issue.

Carmakers and unions have lobbied hard for a slower transition, saying the targets outpace actual customer demand.

Reynolds also said that the government was sometimes prepared to invest “alongside” industry.

In 2024, the new Labour government under Keir Starmer agreed to invest £500m in another Tata business, the Port Talbot steelworks, to build greener electric arc furnaces. However, the investment did not prevent 2,500 job losses at the south Wales site.

The prospect of a jobs purge at JLR poses a challenge for Burnham, who has placed plans to “reindustrialise” Britain at the heart of his offer to voters since taking office less than two months ago.

Last year, after JLR suffered the crippling cyber-attack, the government agreed to provide the company with a guaranteed loan facility of £1.5bn to help battle the impact on its supply chains and production. None of the loan has been drawn down.

As well as the cyber-attack, which halted production for several weeks and dented the UK economy, JLR has suffered the fallout from tariffs imposed by Trump, affecting the key American market for models such as the Range Rover and Defender.

Trump initially slapped tariffs of 27.5% on British cars before reducing the figure to 10% as part of a US-UK trade deal unveiled by Starmer to great fanfare at a press conference held at JLR’s Solihull plant in May last year.

Competition from Chinese models such as ​the Jaecoo 7 – ​ranked third among Britain’s top-selling cars – ​has also eaten into sales at JLR, which makes more than 400,000 vehicles a year.

JLR is not alone in being affected by these external factors. The German carmaker Volkswagen said last week it plans to cut a further 50,000 jobs as part of its turnaround plan as it faces US tariffs and Chinese competition.

The Guardian has approached the department for business and trade for comment.

Grab your popcorn as Dan explains why you can't blame Kiffin for creating total havoc in a broken system, as Tim Brando also joins to weigh in on the drama.

What a start to the Lane Kiffin era at LSU. After a week of drama surrounding a couple of players who couldn’t make an NFL roster, the Tigers steamrolled Clemson at home without those players on their roster.

It had it all. A rain delay, an awesome halftime interview, and Lane's first Tiger Walk had to have Screencaps in mind. He was accompanied by Livvy Dunne, Brooks Nader, and Theo Von as he confidently strolled to Saturday's game.

Livvy Dunne and Brooks Nader attend the Fox Upfront 2026 red carpet at New York City Center in New York City on May 11, 2026. (Ben Hider/FOX)

Nader, a Louisiana native, set the tone for the entire day. She was part of the festivities in the morning, and it was clear from that moment on that Clemson didn't stand a chance.

SEC LAWYERS, LANE KIFFIN AND DEATH VALLEY: COLLEGE FOOTBALL’S WEEK 1 IS SET FOR FIREWORKS

She wasn’t there to play around. This was a business trip.

Later in the day came Lane's Tiger Walk and his entourage of Louisiana royalty. Nader returned, having made an outfit change, alongside LSU legend and Nader's "Baywatch" co-star and fellow SI Swimsuit model Livvy Dunne.

A LIST OF THE BEST COLLEGE GAMEDAY SIGNS AT LSU DURING SHOW'S 500TH EPISODE

Why was Theo Von there? Well, he's not, as far as I know, making an appearance in either "Baywatch" or SI Swimsuit, but he is a Louisiana native and evidently a friend of Kiffin's.

With an entrance like that, you had better win convincingly. We're talking 50-plus in a one-sided game where Clemson fans were at home tapping out. A 51-10 beat down works.

Something tells me they're going to have a lot of fun in Baton Rouge this season.

Now to another team who allowed points to be scored on them in Week 1. I get it not every team can dominate at home to open the season and manhandle a lesser opponent without allowing them to score a single point like Penn State did.

Some teams need a second to appear on a clock out of thin air. Teams like No. 16 Michigan who struggled and lost the game to Western Michigan until a second that had already ticked off the game clock returned from the dead.

After that miracle, the Wolverines won the game (asterisk) on a second Hail Mary attempt after the first was thrown out of the back of the end zone and showed the game clock at zero before anyone touched the ball.

Western Michigan was robbed. As sad of a game as it was for Michigan, fans storming the field after such an atrocious performance tells you exactly where they are as a football program.

This might count as a win in the record books, but this is a loss to everyone else.

They’ll be served up with fresh asparagus and a couple of large taters slathered with butter, sour cream and chives.

articles.title: German startup sends first commercial rocket into space from Europe
articles.excerpt:
Isar Aerospace plans rapid expansion amid race to capitalise on expanding satellite-launch market

A German startup has launched the first commercial rocket to reach orbit from continental Europe, a m...
articles.body_text:
Isar Aerospace plans rapid expansion amid race to capitalise on expanding satellite-launch market

A German startup has launched the first commercial rocket to reach orbit from continental Europe, a milestone for Europe’s efforts to secure independent access to space.

Isar Aerospace said on Sunday that it would rapidly ⁠expand satellite deployments after the ⁠first orbital launch of ​its uncrewed Spectrum rocket from Arctic Norway, marking a ⁠breakthrough for a region where several countries are seeking a foothold in the fast-growing market for satellite launches.

“Launch capability is right now the biggest bottleneck in the entire industry,” Isar co-founder and CEO Daniel Metzler told reporters.

Friedrich Merz, the German chancellor, hailed Saturday’s launch in a ​statement, calling it “the beginning of a new era”.

Merz visited Isar’s ‌launch site in March, underscoring Europe’s ‌efforts to establish greater autonomy as the global order once championed by the US is shifting under the administration of country’s president, Donald Trump.

The EU defence and space commissioner, Andrius Kubilius, wrote on the social media platform X: “Europe’s independent access to space just got a major boost.”

Blasting off from Andøya Spaceport, Spectrum carried five small satellites along with an in-flight technology experiment.

It was Isar’s second launch, coming 18 months after the company’s first rocket plunged into the sea and exploded in a fiery spectacle shortly after takeoff from the same site.

Isar has said it already has five more rockets in production and is now focused on scaling up operations to meet rising demand, with a long-term goal of conducting about 40 launches a year.

The German company ​is developing a second launch site in Nova Scotia in eastern Canada.

Global players ⁠in the satellite launch market include Elon Musk’s SpaceX, which launches from the US, and the French firm ArianeGroup, ​a joint venture between Airbus and Safran ​that uses a spaceport in French Guiana, South America.

articles.body_text:
The Reform UK leader is under pressure after senior aides appeared to plot how to bypass electoral laws on foreign donations

In an interview with the BBC’s Laura Kuenssberg, Nigel Farage acknowledged that the comments by James Orr and Dan Jukes were “injudicious at best” and admitted that the optics of the undercover filming don’t look good for his party.

“This looks bad, as does the sale of peerages, as does government contracts for donations. We are not the first people to be involved in a row over donations,” he said.

The BBC aired the full interview during its politics show on Sunday, having released an excerpt of it on Saturday.

In an earlier post, we mentioned that thousands of jobs are to be cut at Jaguar Land Rover (JLR) as the British carmaker slashes costs after a slump in sales. My colleague Angus Thomson has more details about the expected job cuts in this story. Here is an extract from the report:

double quotation markJLR informed workers and their union on Saturday that the company would be opening a voluntary redundancy programme for salaried and management team members, the BBC and Sunday Times reported.

As many as 4,000 jobs would be cut over two years, the Times reported. JLR told the BBC it was yet to confirm the number but the company, which is owned by the Indian conglomerate Tata Motors, needed to save about £1.7bn over the next two years.

Unite’s general secretary, Sharon Graham, told the BBC she and the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, would meet JLR’s chief executive, PB Balaji, next week, after a weekend of intensive talks to mitigate job losses.

About 30,000 of the company’s 44,000 employees are based in the UK. Most of them work at 14 plants across the West Midlands, where the company is one of the region’s largest employers.

Sagal Abdi-Wali arrived in Camden as a child refugee from Somalia. She has worked for more than a decade as a volunteer and trustee for local charities and is a governor of two schools in the borough, according to Labour.

She was first elected as a councillor in 2022 and became the leader of the council in May, when she said: “Camden has been my home for 35 years. It is the place that gave my family sanctuary, that welcomed us, and that has shaped so much of who I am, what I stand for and what inspired my commitment to public service and to working for the community that welcomed us.”

Labour is expected to announce its candidate for the Holborn and St Pancras byelection by Wednesday. It faces a battle against the Green party to retain the seat as Zack Polanski, its leader in England and Wales, is expected to be confirmed as its candidate.

Zia Yusuf, Reform UK’s home affairs spokesperson, has been accused of “pretty straightforward racism” by a Cabinet minister over comments about a potential Labour byelection candidate who was born in Somalia.

Yusuf has been criticised for a tweet about Sagal Abdi-Wali, a former child refugee and the leader of Camden council, who has been tipped as a favourite to stand for Labour in the Holborn and St Pancras contest triggered by former prime minister Keir Starmer’s resignation as an MP.

Yusuf wrote on X last week: “The front runner being foisted on the people of Holborn by Labour to replace the former Prime Minister Keir Starmer in our Parliament was born in Somalia. Do you understand what’s happening?”

The business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, was asked what he thought of Yusuf’s tweet during an interview with Jon Sopel on Sky News this morning.

“Pretty straightforward racism, isn’t it?” Reynolds said, adding that the potential Labour candidate had “spent decades in this country” and made a “huge contribution to her local community”.

Robert Jenrick, Reform’s economic spokesperson, later denied his colleague’s comments were racist and suggested it was legitimate to question the loyalties of foreign-born candidates.

“I don’t know this person, so I’m not here to cast aspersions upon her, but I do want people to sit in our parliament who are entirely committed to our country,” Jenrick said.

Javier Milei’s threats to the Falkland Islands make it even more important that Andy Burnham increase defence spending immediately, according to the Labour chair of the defence committee.

Tan Dhesi said the comments by the Argentinian president this week show why the government should raise military spending to 3% of GDP by 2030.

But he said Burnham’s plans remain mired in confusion after the prime minister appeared to reassure him that the 2030 target would be hit, only for Downing Street to later retreat.

“It’s important the prime minister and the chancellor don’t defer those decisions to next year,” Dhesi told the Guardian.

“We’ve seen Germany publicly expose Russia for the drone incident [in Leipzig]. Now we’ve got a threat from Argentina saying they are looking to take over the Falklands. We owe it to the Falklands – they say it’s their right to self-determination. It’s important that we also defend them from this threat.”

Reform UK’s Robert Jenrick also condemned the disruption of the Port of Dover by masked demonstrators – but said he understood the frustration with small boats crossing the Channel. Speaking to Sky News’ Sunday Morning programme, Reform’s economic spokesperson said:

double quotation markI absolutely do. I’ve always hated people obstructing other people doing their daily life, whether it’s Just Stop Oil or whatever.

And I don’t like people going around in balaclavas, which is obviously very intimidating. In fact, our party’s policy is to ban face coverings like that.

But do I understand why people are extremely frustrated? Yes, absolutely. This needs to end. This farce of the small boats has been going on for far too long.

And in fact you saw at our conference Nigel Farage and (National Rally president) Jordan Bardella, the likely next prime minister of France, signing an agreement which has the prospect of ending this once and for all.

Channel crossings are down about 40% compared to last year, with the number of crossings this summer at their lowest level since 2019. Home Office data shows people in small boats overwhelmingly come from war and conflict zones.

Reform UK’s Nigel Farage has agreed a deal with France’s hard-right National Rally party on returning migrants who try to cross the Channel in small boats, if both parties achieve power. A Labour party spokesperson said the proposal “is a meaningless document packed with daft and dangerous ideas, signed by an increasingly disgraced Reform leader and an opposition politician. It is nothing more than pointless posturing.”

The business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, went on to condemn the hundreds of masked protesters who prevented traffic from coming in and out of the port of Dover yesterday. In the interview with the BBC, he praised the police for effectively dealing with the “intimidatory behaviour” and said he had sympathy for the “people around Dover” and those disrupted by the delays.

A group called Patriot Platform, which styles itself as having “a fierce love for our homeland”, claimed responsibility for the blockade, as my colleagues note in this story.

The far-right activist Tommy Robinson, whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, reposted videos of the blockade, highlighting a live stream of the protest that directed viewers towards Patriot Platform.

Thousands of workers at Jaguar Land Rover (JLR) will be offered redundancies with job losses reported to be spread over two years. The job cuts will be unwelcome news for Andy Burnham, who has vowed to “safeguard sovereign manufacturing” and reindustrialise Britain.

When asked if the government would be willing to protect the jobs, the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, said it is not for him to “intervene” as he isn’t responsible for running JLR’s business.

“They need to know what the right footprint for them going forward is. I want to talk to them about the numbers,” Reynolds told the BBC, adding there could be financial support for long-term investment but not for a taxpayer-funded bailout.

Farage claims that he faces a disproportionate level of scrutiny compared to the other parties. When Laura Kuenssberg gave the Reform leader a series of examples of investigations faced by other party leaders, Farage responded:

double quotation markI don’t think the others have been de-banked. I don’t think the others have been kicked out by their pension provider. I don’t think the others have literally had an attempt to wipe them out of society, oh and their families as well.

There is no doubt there is huge political prejudice against Reform right across the corporate world and right across the establishment. And that is a simple fact of life – and why? Because we are the disrupters and that’s the way it works.

Farage told the Daily T podcast last month that he had received about 400 death threats in the last seven weeks, and as a high-profile, extremely divisive politician, it is argued that he needs a high level of security.

The claim that Reform is fighting the establishment is undermined by the fact that many of his senior figures, including treasury spokesperson Robert Jenrick and the MP for Fareham and Waterlooville, Suella Braverman, are former Conservative cabinet ministers who were at the heart of the same political establishment Farage is railing against.

In an interview with the BBC’s Laura Kuenssberg, Nigel Farage acknowledged that the comments by James Orr and Dan Jukes were “injudicious at best” and admitted that the optics of the undercover filming don’t look good for his party.

“This looks bad, as does the sale of peerages, as does government contracts for donations. We are not the first people to be involved in a row over donations,” he said.

The BBC aired the full interview during its politics show on Sunday, having released an excerpt of it on Saturday.

The Guardian’s city editor, Anna Isaac, is sitting on the panel on Laura Kuenssberg’s show alongside broadcaster Jeremy Vine and political scientist Francis Fukuyama.

Her revelation that Nigel Farage received a £5m gift from the Thailand-based crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne shortly before announcing he would stand in the 2024 British general election has dogged the Reform leader ever since she broke the story in April.

Farage, who has given different explanations as to why he accepted the gift, has argued he did not need to declare the money because he received it before he was elected as Clacton MP and it “wasn’t political in any sense at all”.

The parliamentary standards commissioner is investigating whether he broke the rules.

Isaac’s report came before a series of other stories raising questions about Reform’s finances, some of which you can read here. Isaac was among the journalists who have reported critically on Reform who were banned from the party’s annual conference this year.

Good morning and welcome to our live coverage of UK politics. The Reform UK party leader, Nigel Farage, is scheduled to appear in an interview on Laura Kuenssberg’s Sunday politics programme at 9am, where he will likely be asked more about an undercover investigation broadcast by Channel 4 News which showed two of his senior aides appearing to plot to get around electoral laws on foreign donations.

Accepting donations from a foreign company, including donations in kind such as polling, could constitute a criminal offence and the party has been reported to the police.

Senior aide Dan Jukes and Reform’s head of policy James Orr have both stood down pending the outcome of an internal party investigation.

As my colleagues note in the story, Farage himself remains under pressure over a separate clip in which he was heard saying “it’s all above board” after one of the reporters who was posing as the UK-based son of a wealthy US backer told the Reform leader he had been in discussions with Jukes and Orr for some time.

“I’ll be the registered donor,” the son says. “But then dad will send the money to me, and then as soon as that’s done and all those conversations are had the money is available.”

On Saturday, during the party’s conference in Birmingham, Farage continued to bat away suggestions of impropriety. “I’m not a compliance officer,” he told the BBC. “I frankly wasn’t even listening,” he said in reference to the meeting with the undercover reporters in Clacton.

Farage has framed the investigation, carried out by Verbatim Investigations, which was founded by journalists from the Centre for Climate Reporting, as another example of an establishment stitch up, and has denied any wrongdoing, as have Orr and Jukes.

articles.title: Farage says overseas donation row ‘looks bad’ but denies Reform breached electoral law
articles.excerpt:
Robert Jenrick says party has followed legal protocol ‘at all times’ as Met police consider launching investigation

Nigel Farage has acknowledged the overseas donation row engulfing Reform UK “looks ...
articles.body_text:
Robert Jenrick says party has followed legal protocol ‘at all times’ as Met police consider launching investigation

Nigel Farage has acknowledged the overseas donation row engulfing Reform UK “looks bad” for his party but denied it had ever taken foreign money in breach of electoral law.

The Reform leader, who is battling to contain the fallout from the allegations, was asked to categorically rule out that foreign money had ever been funnelled to his party. He replied: “I can … never happened.”

Farage was forced to suspend his close aide Dan Jukes and Reform’s head of policy, James Orr, on Friday after they were filmed in an undercover investigation apparently plotting to get around electoral laws on foreign donations.

In an interview with the BBC’s Laura Kuenssberg, Farage described their comments as “injudicious at best” and admitted the optics of the undercover filming were problematic for his party, which has in the past tried to suggest it would do politics differently.

“This looks bad, as does the sale of peerages, as does government contracts for donations,” he said. “We are not the first people to be involved in a row over donations.”

The Metropolitan police are now assessing the evidence after a complaint that Farage and his aides have broken political funding laws, with sources suggesting a full investigation is expected to be launched. They all deny wrongdoing.

Scotland Yard could extend an existing investigation into whether Reform took donations channelled through an intermediary from potentially impermissible sources, which the party and donors deny.

Farage is already facing intense scrutiny about Reform’s finances, as well as a £5m gift by a crypto billionaire shortly before announcing he would stand in the 2024 general election, which he has since said was intended to pay for security.

In an earlier extract of the BBC interview, Farage also claimed he “wasn’t even listening” during the meeting at the centre of the controversy, and that he knew donation law “better than anybody”, as he sought to limit the damage caused by the allegations.

Robert Jenrick, Reform’s Treasury spokesperson, said on Sunday that he had seen legal advice that the party had not in fact broken electoral law over foreign donations but that lessons would be learned from the episode.

“We’re going to investigate exactly what happened,” Jenrick told Sky News. “It’s right to have due process. But this is not the way that Reform conducts itself.

“Like any political party, we seek to abide by the law at all times, and we believe we have in this case. In fact, I’ve reviewed the legal advice from the KC who’s advised the party in the last 48 hours, and it shows that, yeah, we did.

“But do we want for the best version of ourselves? Yes, absolutely. And no doubt there will be lessons to be learnt from this.”

Speaking after the BBC interview, the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, said: “For a political party that don’t like foreigners much they do seem to have a soft spot for foreign cash. We have rules in this country about how our democracy works and everyone has to stick to them.”

He added: “I think you see someone struggling to decide whether they’re really serious about trying to run for power or want to keep the protest going.”

articles.body_text:
‘My View with Lara Trump’ host Lara Trump discusses the Democratic Party’s progressive shift, their use of social media to target young voters and more on ‘Fox & Friends Weekend.’

Democrats have made summer pilgrimages to Nantucket, tapping the wealthy Massachusetts island’s donor class as candidates and party leaders stockpile campaign cash ahead of November.

Nantucket and neighboring Martha’s Vineyard have long been magnets for political fundraising, and Democrats are again tapping the islands’ deep-pocketed donor networks as candidates and party leaders build their war chests ahead of November’s midterm elections.

As of June 30, the Democratic National Committee, Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee and Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee had about $136 million in combined cash on hand, compared with roughly $277 million held by their Republican counterparts, according to federal filings.

This summer, House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., Texas Senate candidate James Talarico, Rep. Seth Moulton, D-Mass., and others have been spotted on the island for fundraising events.

FOX NEWS POWER RANKINGS: AS DEMOCRATS TURN LEFT, BLACK VOTERS TAP THE BRAKES

To salvage the annual event, another church on the island, St. Paul’s Episcopal Church, announced it would read the Declaration of Independence and the Bill of Rights. (Ashley J. DiMella/Fox News Digital)

Sen. Jon Ossoff, D-Ga., reportedly went to Nantucket for an Aug. 29 fundraiser hosted by Democratic heavyweight Elizabeth Frawley Bagley, a Biden-appointed U.S. ambassador to Brazil who previously served as ambassador to Portugal under President Bill Clinton, according to the Boston Globe.

The Democratic fundraising circuit extends to neighboring Martha's Vineyard, another exclusive Massachusetts vacation destination.

Former President Barack Obama visited Martha's Vineyard on Aug. 31 for an event hosted by former Attorney General Eric Holder benefiting the National Democratic Redistricting Committee.

Wes Moore, a possible 2028 presidential contender, was on Martha’s Vineyard the weekend of Aug. 8 for a DNC fundraiser with DNC Chair Ken Martin.

"Where was Wes Moore last weekend? Not campaigning in Maryland or solving our problems in Annapolis, but speaking at a national Democrat event in Martha’s Vineyard. Wes Moore's priority isn’t Maryland, and it will never be Maryland. His only focus is growing his national profile and running for President in 2028. Elect Dan Cox for a Governor who will put Maryland and the needs of Marylanders first," wrote Maryland GOP at the time.

Iowa state Rep. Josh Turek, a Democratic nominee for the open Senate seat held by retiring Republican Sen. Joni Ernst, was spotted on Nantucket while the Iowa State Fair was still underway. Turek, had appeared at the fair earlier in the week, did not answer a reporter’s questions about his fundraising stop, according to videos on social media.

Democratic donors Frank Herron and Sandra Urie, who previously hosted then-first lady Jill Biden for a 2022 Democratic National Committee fundraiser at their Nantucket home, hosted Moulton for a Nantucket fundraising brunch on August 2, according to local paper Nantucket Current.

JON OSSOFF DODGES ON WHY HE INVOKED TRUMP AIDE'S NAME DURING GEORGIA CAMPAIGN RALLY

Shot of Jeep with Trump sticker outside of rose covered cottage on Sconset, Nantucket. (Ashley J. DiMella/Fox News Digital)

Michelle Obama was also on the island, on Aug. 23, but was there to promote her book, "The Look," at two sold-out conversations at the Performing Arts Center in Oak Bluffs. The Obama's have had a vacation house on the Vineyard since 2019.

Nantucket has long been a destination for prominent Democrats as well as celebrities, millionaires and billionaires.

Former President Joe Biden and his family have traveled to the island for decades to celebrate Thanksgiving.

Former first lady Jill Biden was also spotted on the island in July to promote her new book, "View From the East Wing: A Memoir."

DEM ATTORNEY BACKS GOP HOPEFUL IN MICHIGAN RACE AGAINST EL-SAYED, 'JUMPING SHIP' FROM HIS PARTY'S 'LUNATICS'

President Joe Biden carries a milkshake while visiting Nantucket for the Thanksgiving holiday in 2023. (BRENDAN SMIALOWSKI/AFP via Getty Images)

Republicans have also tapped Nantucket’s deep-pocketed donor circuit. Back in 2022, when Vice President JD Vance was running for Senate, he appeared alongside Florida Senator Rick Scott and fellow Senate candidates Ted Budd, Dr. Mehmet Oz and Herschel Walker for another fundraising jaunt on the affluent island.

The NDRC is focusing on key battlegrounds including Arizona, Georgia, Michigan, North Carolina, Ohio, Pennsylvania, Texas and Wisconsin.

Ashley J. DiMella reports on politics for Fox News Digital.

articles.title: Far-right AfD predicted to win big in crucial German state election
articles.excerpt:
Polling stations open in Saxony-Anhalt with anti-immigration party AfD predicted to gain 41% vote share

Polls have opened in the east German state of Saxony-Anhalt, where the populist, far-right, ant...
articles.body_text:
Polling stations open in Saxony-Anhalt with anti-immigration party AfD predicted to gain 41% vote share

Polls have opened in the east German state of Saxony-Anhalt, where the populist, far-right, anti-immigration Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) is predicted to emerge on top in an election that could have a groundbreaking effect on Germany’s political landscape.

About 1.7 million people are eligible to vote. Polling booths opened at 8am local time and will close at 6pm, when exit polls are expected to deliver an initial indication of whether the AfD has secured enough votes for an absolute majority, enabling it to govern the state.

That would mark the first time the party had won a state government, and the first time since the second world war that a rightwing extremist party had gained power at regional state or parliament level in Germany.

Final polls ahead of the vote showed the AfD to have about 40-41% of support. The number of undecided voters in advance of the vote was much lower than at previous elections, polling showed.

Currently, the small state is governed by the conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) of Chancellor Friedrich Merz, together with two smaller parties. The CDU, on about 23%, under its state prime minister, Sven Schulze, hopes to be able to construct a multiparty coalition to be able to retain power.

The CDU and all other mainstream parties have refused to be in coalition with the AfD in a government, in what is referred to as a Brandmauer or firewall. The AfD in Saxony-Anhalt has been classed as “rightwing extremist” by Germany’s domestic intelligence agency.

The AfD’s lead candidate is Ulrich Siegmund, 35, a photogenic former fragrance salesman with a large following on TikTok who has been celebrated like a pop star.

He has insisted he will only take power if the party receives an absolute majority, and would not tolerate a coalition with another party.

The Saxony-Anhalt election is the biggest test yet for Merz, who is very unpopular, along with his government, having failed in his promises to reset Germany’s struggling economy and reduce the support for the AfD. Irregular immigration has reduced since he has been in office, but not to the extent that it has appeased the average voter.

If the AfD won convincingly, it would put huge pressure on Merz. In national polls, the CDU has also been overtaken by the AfD, which has its eyes on victory at the next federal election in 2029.

If the AfD is elected in Saxony-Anhalt, Siegmund has promised to start a remigration and deportation offensive, ban rainbow flags in schools and halt the building of new wind farms.

He wants to change the slogan of the state from “Think modern” to “Think German” and to reintroduce the singing of the national anthem in schools.

Siegmund has sought to capitalise on a mood of ostalgie – nostalgia for communist East Germany – and to tap into discontent amongst east Germans who view themselves as second-class citizens, compared to people from the west.

He turned up to vote on Sunday morning with his wife, riding an East German-era moped in the party colours, which was also a prominent prop during the election campaign in rallies across the state. In a statement in front of the polling station, he voiced his optimism that the party would achieve “45%, and some”.

Thousands of opponents of the AfD gathered in the state capital, Magdeburg, on Saturday for a “festival of democracy”.

On Saturday evening, a message beamed onto the facade of Magdeburg Cathedral read: “We do not abandon what we love. True love of the homeland is not the AfD.”

The bishop of Magdeburg, Gerhard Feige, in an address to a gathering of churchgoers, warned against forces “that want to sow discord, stoke mistrust and fear”. He drew parallels to historical developments, warning that a democracy has the potential to abolish itself. “Not everyone who votes or is elected democratically is a democrat,” he said.

The German Economic Institute has warned of the far-reaching consequences for the German economy, in Saxony-Anhalt and beyond, specifically over its immigration policy, which it said would be “calamitous” for the state, which has an ageing, dwindling population and is heavily dependent on foreign workers.

Critics have also warned that an AfD-run state, due to the Kremlin-friendly stance of the party, could leak sensitive information to Russia. The AfD has dismissed such claims. It has said it would seek to reform the domestic intelligence service, calling it biased.

The latest poll by the public broadcaster ZDF on Thursday put the AfD on a decisive lead of 41%, with the CDU trailing on 23%, the far-left Die Linke on 11.5%, the Social Democrats on 8.5% and the Greens on 6%. Two smaller parties failed to reach the 5% hurdle needed to re-enter parliament.

Independent election observers are active at polling booths amid speculation from the AfD that voter fraud has taken place, in particular in postal voting, with specific focus on a retirement home. State authorities have denied the claims.

articles.title: US, Iran engaged in tanker war: Where is the months-long conflict headed?
articles.excerpt: The United States and Iran have escalated tit-for-tat attacks in the past 24 hours, with Washington targeting three Iranian oil tankers and Tehran hitting tankers and firing a ballistic missile toward...
articles.body_text:
The United States and Iran have escalated tit-for-tat attacks in the past 24 hours, with Washington targeting three Iranian oil tankers and Tehran hitting tankers and firing a ballistic missile towards US warships patrolling near the Strait of Hormuz.

Experts have dubbed Iran’s targeting of the two US aircraft carriers a “calculated escalation”, as the months-long fighting is increasingly playing out at sea, with both sides trying to exert control over the strategic strait – a global chokepoint used by Tehran as leverage in the war.

The attacks on tankers come as the US claims that an increasing volume of oil has started to flow through the strait, though the exact figures are still debatable, while the naval blockade of Iranian ports continues.

The latest exchanges further dim hopes for a de-escalation through diplomacy as the US-Israel war on Iran has disrupted energy supplies and slowed economic growth around the world.

So, what do we know about the latest tanker wars, and where is the conflict headed?

US Central Command (CENTCOM) said its forces struck three Iranian vessels, including a tanker off Kharg Island, the hub through which Iran exported 90 percent of its crude before the war.

Another tanker was struck near Jask, and an unladen vessel was hit in the Gulf of Oman after its crew was told to abandon ship.

CENTCOM said the attacks followed Iranian ballistic missile launches against a US aircraft carrier and navy destroyer, which it said successfully evaded the strikes. No US personnel were injured.

“If you shoot at two of our ships, we will impose an even higher economic cost — taking out three of yours,” CENTCOM commander Admiral Brad Cooper said.

Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said it launched “several ballistic missiles” at the aircraft carrier and destroyer, accusing them of “harassing Iranian ships” and taking part in a naval blockade.

“The Iranians did not only target two ordinary warships – they targeted a missile destroyer and, remarkably, an aircraft carrier … the backbone of the American campaign against Iran,” defence analyst Wolfgang Pusztai told Al Jazeera.

“This is a very, very significant development, and it doesn’t come as a surprise that the Americans retaliated.”

Iran then said its forces also targeted three oil tankers travelling through what it called an “unauthorised route” in the Strait of Hormuz and three US-linked vessels elsewhere.

In a statement carried by Iranian broadcaster IRIB, the IRGC navy warned all vessels in the Gulf or near the Strait of Hormuz not to be “deceived” by the US military and to “refrain from any suspicious movement aimed at transiting unauthorised waterways”.

“Otherwise, you will be targeted,” it said.

On Sunday, Iran claimed it struck an unmanned US vessel trying to enter the Strait of Hormuz, according to The Associated Press news agency.

Washington claimed the Iranian tankers it struck were part of a multibillion-dollar shadow network financing the IRGC and its regional allies.

Iran has long relied partly on a shadow fleet to circumvent sanctions and sell oil, a source of revenue that has become more important since the US began blockading Iranian ports in April.

Iran effectively shut the Strait of Hormuz, through which 20 percent of the world’s oil supplies flowed, in retaliation for the US-Israeli attacks that began on February 28. Some 20 million barrels of oil flowed daily before the war began.

Hassan Ghashghavi, a lawmaker and spokesman for the Iranian Parliament’s National Security Commission, said the attacks on US warships were part of “an existential war with America”, arguing that Washington’s naval blockade “should never have existed” in the first place.

“Naturally, they have acted militarily in violation of all international laws,” he told Al Jazeera, adding that “because America is far from us, it does not see this war as existential”.

Meanwhile, the US has continued to build pressure on Iran to open the key waterway, both militarily and economically.

Last month, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced a raft of economic measures to target Tehran’s financial interests across the world.

Bessent said the US would target all of Iran’s sources of revenue, including oil, to prevent other countries and companies from doing business with Tehran.

This comes despite US assertions of normalcy in the Strait of Hormuz, with Washington insisting the waterway is open and that dozens of ships carrying millions of barrels of oil transit it each day.

Last week, Bessent claimed that some 17 million barrels of crude oil a day had been shipped out recently, according to a report in the United Kingdom’s The Times newspaper. Al Jazeera, however, could not independently verify the claims in the report.

President Donald Trump claimed last month that the US was in “total control” of the strait.

Yet figures from marine analytics firm Kpler show only six vessels crossed the strait on Wednesday, 11 on Tuesday and five on Monday, with a 10-day average of just 13 vessels per day.

The attacks are adding to concerns about global energy supplies.

Brent crude futures closed on Friday at $96.28 a barrel, their highest level since July 24, up from roughly $70 before the war.

Predictably, US oil and gas prices have also skyrocketed, coming at a crucial time for Trump as Americans head to the polls for midterm elections in November.

Diesel hit a new record price in the US on Friday, soaring to an average of $5.85 a gallon ($1.55 per litre) for the first time ever. Polls have repeatedly suggested a majority of Americans oppose the war, which has also plunged Trump’s popularity.

A Reuters/Ipsos survey conducted in late August found that only 31 percent of Americans back the war, while 63 percent are against it.

The same polling suggested Trump’s approval rating has dropped to 33 percent, down from 40 percent since the fighting began.

The renewed exchanges of strikes between Iran and the US mark an escalation in the six-month-long conflict, according to the director of the Middle East studies programme at George Washington University, Sina Azodi.

Azodi told Al Jazeera that neither side will “cave in” because it “will not look good on them, so the only option is to escalate”.

He said unless there is a political settlement, the war will continue.

“There’s going to be more clashes between the Iranians and the Americans. There can be miscalculations. There can be more civilian casualties”, especially on the Iranian side, Azodi said.

“The [US] secretary of defence can send more troops to the region, but I don’t think the Iranians are going to back down. They’re going to resist that blockade and impose further costs on the United States.”

He said the goal of the US and Iran is to force the other to back down. “The winner is going to be the one that can accept more costs and punishment,” Azodi said.

Commenting on Iran’s strategy, Ali Akbar Dareini, an analyst at the Center for Strategic Studies in Tehran, echoed Azodi, saying the US attacks on Iranian oil tankers are a “big issue” that Iran cannot afford to let “go unanswered”.

“Does it make Iran surrender? No, it compels Iran. It incentivises Iran to lash out and retaliate” more harshly, Dareini told Al Jazeera.

He said the US naval blockade, coupled with sanctions, is inflicting severe pain on Iran, but added the latter has plans to counter it. Iran cannot tolerate this naval blockade to continue, so Iran is already making preparations to break the siege.

“At the same time, Iran definitely has its own plans to make sure that oil prices will shoot up over $100 per barrel,” Dareini said.

articles.title: Black-clad Dover protesters condemned for ‘dressing up in costumes’ by minister
articles.excerpt:
Business secretary says masked anti-immigration protest was ‘not something we would want’ on British streets

A cabinet minister has condemned the blocking of Dover roads by dozens of masked and black...
articles.body_text:
Business secretary says masked anti-immigration protest was ‘not something we would want’ on British streets

A cabinet minister has condemned the blocking of Dover roads by dozens of masked and black-clad people on Saturday.

Jonathan Reynolds, the business secretary, said that although peaceful protest was an “essential part of British life”, this differed from “dressing up in costumes like this and disrupting people’s lives”.

He told the Sky News Sunday Morning programme: “So I would condemn it, but I’d condemn the disruption it caused for local people as well.”

Adding that the situation had been resolved, he said: “Clearly, that’s not something we would want or expect to see on the [streets] of Britain.”

He declined to comment “on the security and policing side of it”, but when pressed on the apparent unpreparedness of the police, he said he thought that “on the whole, the police handled it very well”.

Responsibility for the demonstration appears to have been claimed by Patriot Platform, an anti-immigration group with links to the far right which styles itself as having a “fierce love for our homeland”.

Kent police attended and engaged with the protest on Saturday, which the Port of Dover described as a “public order incident”. Protesters had dispersed by lunchtime, and no arrests were made during the incident.

Traffic in and out of the port on the A20 was stopped, causing delays of up to 45 minutes and four miles of congestion, according to National Highways. Videos shared online showed masked people in black marching on the road in a group as lorries waited in traffic next to police cars. The number of people involved was not immediately clear, and police did not give an official estimate. One livestreamer estimated that he was marching with hundreds of people.

Social media videos showed demonstrators linking arms in a blockade across the A20, chanting “stop the boats” and “England till I die”.

Mike Tapp, the Labour MP for Dover and Deal, posted on X: “A clearly coordinated protest is not ‘spontaneous’ as described by Police. We can and must do better.”

He noted that Kent police appeared to have had “little advance warning”, and questioned whether intelligence had been missed. “I will be asking why,” he wrote.

“Concerns around illegal migration are not racist. I’ve said that many times. But what we saw today in Dover is against our laws and not fair on residents.”

In a piece for the Mirror, Tapp suggested that he would like additional officers, including mutual aid from forces such as the Met, mobilised quickly if Dover is targeted again.

He wrote: “The Port of Dover is not just another road junction. It is critical national infrastructure, handling around a third of UK trade in goods with the EU and huge volumes of roll-on, roll-off freight. When Dover stops, Britain feels it.

“And the law matters. Wilfully obstructing a highway can be a criminal offence. New legislation also means police can designate protest areas where concealing your identity with a balaclava or other face covering becomes an offence.”

A government spokesperson said: “The right to peaceful protest is fundamental to our democracy, but we condemn the behaviour in Dover and the travel disruption it has caused.”

articles.title: Palestinians in Gaza bury remains of 100 people recovered from rubble
articles.excerpt: Palestinians in northern Gaza are holding funeral ceremonies for about 100 people, including 60 children, whose remains were recovered from the rubble of destroyed buildings in Gaza City’s Zeitoun nei...
articles.body_text:
Palestinians in northern Gaza are holding funeral ceremonies for about 100 people, including 60 children, whose remains were recovered from the rubble of destroyed buildings in Gaza City’s Zeitoun neighbourhood.

The remains were carried on Sunday by family members from Zeitoun to al-Ma’madani cemetery in central Gaza City for burial, according to Al Jazeera’s correspondent at the scene, Ghazi al-Aloul.

Civil defence crews and family members had spent weeks digging through the ruins of homes hit during Israel’s genocidal war against Palestinians in Gaza, which began in October 2023.

Many of the victims were part of the extended Malaka family, which alone lost 55 members.

Al-Aloul said families had waited a long time to be able to bury their loved ones in “known, proper cemeteries”. He said that the chance to bury the remains of family members was “not available to every family”, noting that Israeli forces had destroyed and dug up cemeteries elsewhere in Gaza during the war.

Al-Aloul said the remains, though wrapped in shrouds resembling intact bodies, were often only fragments.

“These are bone remains and remnants of belongings that may have been found on the bodies, especially the children’s,” he said, adding that no complete bodies had been recovered from the site because “the Israeli occupation has prolonged this process, and continues to prolong it and prevent it from being completed quickly”.

Raed al-Dahshan, head of Gaza’s civil defence service, told Al Jazeera his teams had formulated plans to carry out recovery operations for thousands more missing bodies, but said the work was being held back by a shortage of heavy machinery.

“We don’t have equipment, we don’t have protective equipment” for rescue workers, he told Al Jazeera.

Dahshan said the recovery of an estimated 8,000 bodies still believed to be under rubble could be completed in about 90 days with proper equipment, but “if that equipment is barred from entering Gaza … this work will continue for years”.

He said his agency had submitted a detailed list of needed equipment to international institutions and was willing to have that machinery remain under international control rather than with the civil defence directly.

He said crews needed large excavators, personal protective equipment and search equipment to locate remains urgently.

On identifying remains, he said crews rely on survivors and neighbouring families to establish who was in a building and where they were at the time of the strike, supported by a team of engineers who sort and document findings in the field. He said Israeli forces’ failure to warn residents before strikes meant “dozens, even hundreds” of homes still required excavation.

Ajith Sunghay, head of the UN human rights office in the occupied Palestinian territories, told Al Jazeera that the scenes were a reminder of “the brutality of this conflict”, noting some of the remains dated back to November 2023.

“Thousands of people are still languishing under this rubble … We’re talking about areas that may be under Israeli military control, 70 percent of Gaza – there’s difficulty accessing these areas to extract these bodies.”

“Accountability must happen … It’s essential that we preserve the evidence we’ve been able to obtain during this sensitive period.”

Gaza’s Health Ministry says at least 73,651 Palestinians have been killed and 174,592 wounded since October 2023.

Similar recovery operations in recent weeks have retrieved more than 100 bodies of people from the Abu Shariah and Hassaniya families who were killed in a single strike, as well as more than 500 bodies from the Al-Taj tower site, officials and activists said.

articles.title: MIKE DAVIS: Trump's ballroom win highlights need for serious judicial nominees
articles.excerpt: The Supreme Court has ruled to allow the $400 million White House ballroom construction project to continue in a 5-4 ruling. The decision replaces an order issued earlier in the month that halted cons...
articles.body_text:
The Supreme Court has ruled to allow the $400 million White House ballroom construction project to continue in a 5-4 ruling. The decision replaces an order issued earlier in the month that halted construction in Washington, D.C.

Last year, President Trump ordered construction of a White House ballroom and a secure underground military facility. A DC busybody sued to stop it, and on Aug. 31, the Supreme Court killed this laughable lawsuit by a single vote. Mid-construction, long after the East Wing’s demolition, Chief Justice John Roberts joined the three Democrat women to try to shut down the president of the United States’ security improvement, expressly permitted by federal statute and Article II of the Constitution, to the White House complex. This narrow 5-4 ruling proves precisely why Republicans must continue to nominate and confirm rock-solid constitutionalists all across the federal judiciary.

For decades, the White House hosted large events in outdoor tents, with women’s high heels sinking into the soggy Rose Garden and other White House grounds. But that open setting provides a rich target for terrorists, including too many of today’s Democrats, who wish to harm the president. The threat is all too real. Just over two years ago, Matthew Thomas Crooks nearly assassinated Trump at an open-air campaign rally in Butler, Pa. Two months later, Ryan Routh attempted another assassination of Trump at a Florida golf course. In April, a third would-be assassin attempted to murder Trump in a DC hotel ballroom at the annual White House Correspondents’ Dinner.

The White House helipad and new ballroom extension under construction in Washington, D.C. on Aug. 5, 2026. (Aaron Schwartz/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

The dire need for a highly secure White House ballroom is obvious—and presidents and their guests long after Trump will enjoy its beauty, utility, and convenience. The White House regularly hosts heads of state, members of Congress, foreign diplomats, and other high-value targets of America’s enemies. Any reasonable person ought to know that, in these disturbing times, we need the most enhanced security imaginable. Trump acted. He ordered the demolition of the run-down, long-past-its-prime White House East Wing to build a privately funded, 70-foot-tall indoor ballroom, a subterranean military bunker, and rooftop security facility.

WHITE HOUSE CORRESPONDENTS' DINNER SHOOTING SHARPENS FOCUS ON TRUMP’S BALLROOM CONSTRUCTION PROPOSAL

Enter Alison Hoagland, an underworked DC busybody and member of the National Trust for Historic Preservation, who claims she leisurely strolls by the White House vicinity about once a month —while real Americans, in real America, work real jobs.

She filed suit, claiming the new ballroom was unsightly and offended her apparently very delicate aesthetic sensibilities. DC U.S. District Judge Richard Leon, a George W. Bush appointee who suffers from severe Trump Derangement Syndrome like so many other Republican-appointed DC federal judges, took the bait. He blocked all new above-ground construction for the East Wing unless the subsurface military facility strictly required it.

APPEALS COURT LETS TRUMP RESUME WHITE HOUSE BALLROOM CONSTRUCTION, SEEKS LOWER COURT CLARITY

DC federal judges are legendary for their self-imagined expertise in . . . well, everything. But a judge who has never had a real job in his adult life deluding himself into believing his job is now to moonlight as the construction foreman over the White House complex, instead of the duly-elected president of the United States (who happens to be one of the best builders in the world for over 50 years), is next-level judicial narcissism and lawlessness.

President Donald Trump and Supreme Court Justices Clarence Thomas, center, and Samuel Alito, right. (Chip Somodevilla/Pool/AFP via Getty Images; Andrew Harnik/Getty Images; Matt McClain/The Washington Post via Getty Images)

Unsurprisingly, the Democrat-dominated DC Circuit upheld Leon’s rogue ruling over a superb dissent by U.S. Circuit Judge Neomi Rao, a former law clerk to America’s all-time-greatest Justice Clarence Thomas. The Trump administration took the fight to the Supreme Court, as these DC federal courts would turn the White House complex into a stop-work construction site for years.

TRUMP'S WHITE HOUSE BALLROOM CONSTRUCTION GETS ANOTHER LIFELINE FROM SCOTUS AMID HEATED LEGAL FIGHT

Article III of the U.S. Constitution requires a plaintiff to have standing. In order to bring suit in federal court, a plaintiff needs a concrete, redressable injury that has already occurred or which imminently looms. Plaintiff/DC busybody Alison Hoagland had nothing but her hurt feelings. The High Court has never held that mere personal offense gives someone the right to bring a federal case.

Five of the six Republican-appointed Supreme Court justices correctly rejected Hoagland’s crackpot standing claim. Ruling for her would let anyone file a lawsuit to stop any government building project in America based on aesthetics and hurt feelings. The majority also torched Leon’s unworkable injunction. Leon, the self-appointed construction foreman as even former U.S. Attorney General William Barr —certainly no Trump cheerleader —mocked him , demanded the White House prove every foot of the project served a critical purpose, a subjective standard that would require endless court appearances, construction delays for years, and unnecessary security risks at the White House complex.

Yet Chief Justice John Roberts ignored this basic logic and decided to pen a truly cringeworthy dissent. He argued standing depends on whether a government building is "iconic." He cherry-picked a century-old quote from Theodore Roosevelt to invent a limitless theory of standing. This ludicrous view came within one vote of prevailing. There must be something in the water in these DC federal courthouses.

A McCrery Architects rendering provided by the White House of the new ballroom. (The White House)

Earlier this year, Leon enjoined lawful sanctions against Francesca Albanese, the International Criminal Court’s head prosecutor. The ICC had issued an absurd arrest warrant for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Trump rightfully sanctioned the ICC and its officials. But that didn’t faze Leon. Leon protected Albanese simply because her husband and children hold American citizenship. Thankfully, a D.C. Circuit panel stayed Leon’s stunning injunction, and the sanctions against Albanese remain in effect.

TRUMP SUFFERS MAJOR SUPREME COURT DEFEAT AS JUSTICES UPHOLD BIRTHRIGHT CITIZENSHIP

Roberts’ record is even worse. He cast the deciding vote to uphold Obamacare in 2012, killed the first Trump administration’s U.S. Census citizenship question in 2020, and protected DACA in 2020. He penned a gratuitous concurrence in Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization (2022), explicitly noting he was not voting to overturn Roe v. Wade (1973), one of the worst decisions in Supreme Court history.

This June, Roberts delivered his coup de grâce. He authored Trump v. Barbara, an egregiously wrong opinion constitutionalizing birthright citizenship for the children of illegal immigrants–including 1.5 million (and growing) Chinese birth tourists. Roberts' ruling is the gravest betrayal of our most crucial sovereign power as We The People, the sovereign citizens of America: to control who becomes one of us. Yet Roberts’ ballroom dissent read like a fever dream, following a bad bout of Trump Derangement Syndrome.

JUSTICE THOMAS WARNS PROGRESSIVISM IS A THREAT TO AMERICA IN RARE PUBLIC REMARKS

It could have been worse. Bush put former U.S. Circuit Judge J. Michael Luttig on his Supreme Court short list. This is the same Luttig who advocated throwing Trump off the 2024 ballot under the preposterous theory that he committed "insurrection" on Jan. 6, 2021. That ludicrous argument ultimately didn’t garner a single vote at the Supreme Court—not even from the three Democrat women who generally rule against Trump after simply seeing his name in the case caption.

The Article III Project proudly stands with Trump. We demand staunch constitutionalists in the mold of Justices Clarence Thomas and Samuel Alito. Decades of spineless Republican judges—particularly in the DC swamp--have severely damaged this nation, and the Article III Project will lead the fight to ensure those days never return. Bold and fearless constitutionalists in the mold of new Trump-appointed U.S. Circuit Judge Emil Bove is our future. We won’t get fooled again.

Michael R. Davis is the founder and president of the Article III Project.

articles.title: Zia Yusuf’s post about Camden council leader is ‘straightforward racism’, says minister
articles.excerpt:
Reform UK’s home affairs spokesperson has faced criticism within party after post about Sagal Abdi-Wali, a former child refugee

Labour has accused Reform’s Zia Yusuf of “straightforward racism” after...
articles.body_text:
Reform UK’s home affairs spokesperson has faced criticism within party after post about Sagal Abdi-Wali, a former child refugee

Labour has accused Reform’s Zia Yusuf of “straightforward racism” after he suggested the party’s frontrunner to replace Keir Starmer in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection was not British.

Sagal Abdi-Wali, a former child refugee from Somalia and the leader of Camden council, has been tipped as an early favourite to contest the London seat for Labour after the former prime minister’s resignation.

Yusuf, Reform UK’s home affairs spokesperson, posted on X last week: “The frontrunner being foisted on the people of Holborn by Labour to replace the former prime minister Keir Starmer in our parliament was born in Somalia. Do you understand what’s happening?”

The post, which has been viewed 8m times, drew sharp criticism from several senior Reform UK figures during the party’s conference in Birmingham at the weekend. Appearing on Sky News on Sunday, the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, also condemned Yusuf’s post as “straightforward racism”.

Asked by the presenter, Jon Sopel, for his thoughts on the message, Reynolds said: “Pretty straightforward racism, isn’t it? There’s a potential candidate referenced there; spent decades in this country, huge contribution to her local community, so I think that speaks for itself.”

When Sopel asked whether it was “plain racism”, Reynolds replied: “Absolutely.”

Yusuf has drawn significant criticism for his inflammatory comments on X in recent months, including from top Reform UK figures. Nadine Dorries, the former Conservative minister who defected to Reform UK last year, described the post about Abdi-Wali as “nasty”.

“It was a nasty tweet. Zia Yusuf is a brilliant man, and he’s a genius actually, and he’s an incredible communicator. I wish he closed down his Twitter account,” she told Times Radio.

Laila Cunningham, Reform’s candidate for mayor of London and the daughter of immigrants from Egypt, told the Standard: “I don’t know what he meant by that comment. I read it a few times.

“I didn’t understand what he meant by that comment. Of course, you know, that woman is British. She’s the leader of Camden council. I didn’t understand what he meant by that.”

Reform UK has been contacted for comment.

Abdi-Wali arrived in Camden as a child refugee from Somalia. She has worked for more than a decade as a volunteer and trustee for local charities and is a governor of two schools in the borough, according to Labour.

She was first elected as a councillor in 2022 and became the leader of the council in May, when she said: “Camden has been my home for 35 years. It is the place that gave my family sanctuary, that welcomed us, and that has shaped so much of who I am, what I stand for and what inspired my commitment to public service and to working for the community that welcomed us.”

Labour is expected to announce its candidate for the Holborn and St Pancras byelection by Wednesday. It faces a battle against the Green party to retain the seat as Zack Polanski, its leader in England and Wales, is expected to be confirmed as its candidate.
