articles.title: Legendary agent explains how Deshaun Watson's $230 million contract has crippled the Browns
articles.excerpt:
Famed sports agent Leigh Steinberg talks to OutKick about the fallout of the Cleveland Browns' contract with Deshaun Watson.

The Cleveland Browns hoped when they acquired Deshaun Watson in 2022 that ...
articles.body_text:
Famed sports agent Leigh Steinberg talks to OutKick about the fallout of the Cleveland Browns' contract with Deshaun Watson.

The Cleveland Browns hoped when they acquired Deshaun Watson in 2022 that he would have a major impact on the franchise, and revisiting the trade four years later, they weren’t wrong.

What kind of impact, exactly, has Watson had on the Browns? A disastrous one. The team gave up five draft picks, including three first-rounders, and then signed Watson to a five-year, $230 million fully guaranteed contract, the largest amount of guaranteed money given to a player in NFL history.

Watson was suspended for 11 games in 2022 after facing several sexual assault allegations from his time with the Houston Texans. Watson has played only 19 games in four seasons with the Browns and has disappointed on the field. Legendary sports agent Leigh Steinberg explained that while Watson has hurt the Browns on the field with his play, his exorbitant contract has crippled the team's salary-cap flexibility.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

Cleveland Browns quarterback Deshaun Watson watches from the sidelines against the Las Vegas Raiders in the second half at Allegiant Stadium in Paradise, Nevada, on Nov. 23, 2025. (Kirby Lee/Imagn Images)

"The fact that they've got that contract on Cleveland's roster, which is all guaranteed, makes it very difficult to do what is advanced caponomics, which is to take a high salary, all of which counts against the cap, and supplement it with a new signing bonus and extend the contract out over a series of years," Steinberg told OutKick in a recent interview.

"That's the modus operandi to fit talented players into a cap. But when all the money is guaranteed, there's no way to escape the cap hit."

The Watson contract is so onerous that the Browns were forced to push his cap hit into the future beyond the term of his five-year contract by using void years. Early in Watson’s contract, they lessened his cap hit in order to build around him and pushed a ton of money into the future.

Now they are feeling the constraints of Watson’s deal.

Here are Watson’s cap hits from 2022 through 2030: In 2022, it was $9.4 million, followed by $19 million, nearly $28 million, nearly $36 million and a $40.2 million cap hit this season.

LEGENDARY SPORTS AGENT TALKS ABOUT THE RAMS USE OF 'CAPONOMICS' TO BRING AARON DONALD OUT OF RETIREMENT

Cleveland Browns quarterback Deshaun Watson (4) throws a pass during the first quarter against the Cincinnati Bengals at Huntington Bank Field on Oct. 20, 2024. (Ken Blaze/Imagn Images)

Next season, despite not being on the Browns' roster after his contract expires this season, Watson will have an astronomical $86.2 million cap hit, followed by a $25.7 million cap hit in 2028, nearly $17 million in 2029 and $8.9 million in 2030. In all likelihood, the Browns will have to further leverage their future cap space because carrying an $86.2 million cap charge for a player who will likely not be on their roster next year would be crippling to a front office trying to build a competitive roster.

If the Browns decide to leave that $86.2 million entirely on next season’s cap, it would account for more than a quarter of their salary cap. Despite the cap continuing to rise year after year, a cap hit that high is not tenable for a team trying to win games and spend big in free agency.

The Browns, despite having a 9-10 record in Watson’s starts, named him their Week 1 starting quarterback. Watson has completed 61.2% of his passes for 3,365 yards with 19 touchdowns and 12 interceptions in his tumultuous tenure.

Watson has not played since he tore his right Achilles tendon in October 2024, and re-tore it during rehab in January 2025.

ZERO BS. JUST DAKICH. TAKE THE DON'T @ ME PODCAST ON THE ROAD. DOWNLOAD NOW!

Deshaun Watson of the Cleveland Browns looks to pass during a voluntary veteran minicamp at CrossCountry Mortgage Campus in Berea, Ohio, on April 21, 2026. (Nick Cammett/Getty Images)

The Browns hope Watson can recapture some of the magic he had with the Houston Texans this season under new head coach Todd Monken because, if he can, his massive cap hit won't hurt as much.

But Steinberg isn’t sure Watson will play well enough to fend off backup Shedeur Sanders, and start the whole season.

"Now, if Deshaun Watson were to come back to what he was at Clemson or with Houston, he started out like he was going to have a spectacular career and then because of offseason issues and injuries, the wheels came off. And so, while he's been designated the starter now, it's unclear whether or not he'll hold that till the end of the year," Steinberg said.

Watson is only 30 years old, and Steinberg mentioned quarterbacks who have been effective despite being much older than Watson.

Leigh Steinberg attends the 39th Annual Leigh Steinberg Super Bowl Party at Storek on Feb. 7, 2026 in San Francisco, California. (Jesse Grant/Getty Images)

"He's not too old. As we've seen with Aaron Rodgers and Tom Brady, players can play deep into their 40s and still be effective at that position, but he's got to be a little rusty," Steinberg said.

While the Browns hope Watson can be effective this season, it would come four excruciating seasons later than they would have hoped after giving him the most guaranteed money any player had received in NFL history.

Steinberg, who was inducted into the California Sports Hall of Fame in 2017, has had many high-profile clients throughout his illustrious career. Across football and baseball, Steinberg’s clients include Steve Bartkowski, Steve Young, Troy Aikman, Warren Moon, Bruce Smith, Thurman Thomas, Kordell Stewart, Jeff George, Ben Roethlisberger, Myron Rolle, Matt Leinart, Mark Brunell, Ricky Williams, Howie Long, Eric Karros and Dusty Baker, among others.

Ryan Canfield is a digital production assistant for Fox News Digital.

articles.title: 'Pod Save America' hosts mock JD Vance over ‘blood libel’ definition before botching it themselves
articles.excerpt: "Pod Save America" co-hosts Jon Favreau and Jon Lovett mocked Vice President JD Vance’s use of "blood libel" before offering conflicting explanations of the antisemitic trope. Commentary senior editor...
articles.body_text:
"Pod Save America" co-hosts Jon Favreau and Jon Lovett mocked Vice President JD Vance’s use of "blood libel" before offering conflicting explanations of the antisemitic trope. Commentary senior editor Seth Mandel criticized the exchange.

"Pod Save America" co-hosts Jon Favreau and Jon Lovett mocked Vice President JD Vance during a Wednesday episode for his use of the term "blood libel," only to offer incorrect explanations of the centuries-old antisemitic accusation. They eventually arrived on its historical definition, but drew criticism from Commentary senior editor Seth Mandel.

The hosts laughed while discussing Vance’s usage and suggested he was interpreting the phrase literally through "bloodline" and being "liable," before Lovett offered his own definition.

"The blood libel is that we killed Jesus. That’s it. We killed Jesus," he said.

Pod Save America hosts Jon Favreau and Jon Lovett mocked Vice President JD Vance over his use of "blood libel" before offering conflicting definitions of the antisemitic trope. (Photo by Jerod Harris/Getty Images for Vox Media)

ISRAEL FOREIGN MINISTRY CONDEMNS NEW YORK TIMES PIECE AS 'ONE OF THE WORST BLOOD LIBELS' IN MODERN PRESS

Favreau immediately rejected that explanation but then connected the term to the biblical Passover story in which Israelites marked their doors with lamb’s blood so the plague killing Egypt’s firstborn would pass over their homes.

"No, the blood libel is that Jews supposedly, um, uh, put blood on... this is an Old Testament story... on a house so that when like the angel of death came by, they would skip over the houses with the blood on it but kill the firstborn," he said.

After recognizing that the story was Passover, the hosts eventually read the historical definition of blood libel aloud.

Commentary senior editor Seth Mandel blasted the Pod Save America exchange, accusing the hosts of dismissing antisemitism while misunderstanding the history of blood libel.  (Urs Flueeler, Pool Photo via AP)

VICE PRESIDENT JD VANCE BLASTS MAMDANI, EL-SAYED, AOC AND OSSOFF IN RAPID-FIRE TIKTOK ROAST

Vance explained his understanding of the term while discussing antisemitism before the Republican Jewish Coalition.

"The idea that because of your genetics, because of your blood, because of your ancestry, you are guilty of a crime that you never committed," Vance said. Jewish Insider reported that Vance used "blood libel" and "blood guilt" interchangeably during the appearance.

Mandel said the hosts’ confusion over the meaning of blood libel reflected a broader problem in how accusations of antisemitism are sometimes dismissed, warning that treating Jewish concerns as exaggerated or unserious can both minimize the history behind such tropes and make it easier for antisemitic rhetoric to persist.

"Anti-Semites know how to graft Medieval blood libels onto baseless accusations against Israel and the Jewish community today. The Jewish victims of these blood libels also, of course, know their history quite well. The Pod Save America hosts represent a third group: the self-righteous ignoramuses who automatically dismiss accusations of anti-Semitism against their political allies," Mandel said in a statement to Fox News Digital on Friday.

Favreau and Lovett laughed at Vance’s explanation before confusing blood libel with Jesus’ death and the Passover story, eventually arriving at its historical definition. (Jeff Schear/Getty)

CHRISTIAN LEADERS HOLD EMERGENCY SUMMIT IN JERUSALEM TO CONFRONT GLOBAL RISE IN ANTISEMITISM

"If you start from a position of, essentially, ‘the Jews are silly and oversensitive,’ you will set yourself up to look like a fool, as the Pod bros did. You will also only encourage anti-Semitism to continue, as the Pod bros do," he continued.

The U.S. Holocaust Memorial Museum defines blood libel as the false allegation that Jews used the blood of non-Jews, typically Christian children, for religious rituals. The museum separately identifies the accusation that Jews were collectively responsible for killing Jesus as another historical form of antisemitism.

The Anti-Defamation League (ADL) similarly describes blood libel as the centuries-old falsehood that Jews murdered Christians, particularly children, to use their blood for religious purposes, including the purported baking of Passover matzah. Such accusations historically helped fuel mob violence and pogroms against Jewish communities.

The ADL reported 9,354 incidents of antisemitic assault, harassment and vandalism in the United States in 2024, the highest annual total since the organization began tracking incidents in 1979. The group said 58% of the incidents included elements related to Israel or Zionism, marking the first time such incidents accounted for a majority of its annual tally.

Fox News Digital reached out to Vance for comment, but did not immediately receive a response.

CJ Womack is an associate editor at Fox News.

CJ joined Fox News Digital's team in 2026, which highlights the vital role journalism plays in shaping politics and culture. He has years of experience analyzing and reporting on the news media.

CJ graduated from Long Beach State University in 2025 with a Bachelor of Arts in Political Science and a minor in Journalism.

You can send news tips to cj.womack@fox.com and follow CJ on Twitter.

articles.title: US hits three Iranian oil tankers after saying its warships were targeted
articles.excerpt:
US Central Command released footage of the strikes on Iran-linked tankers

The US military says it has hit three Iran-linked oil tankers after ballistic missiles were launched towards two of its warsh...
articles.body_text:
US Central Command released footage of the strikes on Iran-linked tankers

The US military says it has hit three Iran-linked oil tankers after ballistic missiles were launched towards two of its warships in the region.

US Central Command (Centcom) said on Saturday it had "permanently disabled" a tanker near Kharg Island and another near the Strait of Hormuz, and "completely destroyed" a third in the Gulf of Oman.

Centcom said it "successfully evaded" multiple attacks from the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) targeting a US aircraft carrier and guided-missile destroyer. No American troops were harmed, it said in a statement.

Iranian state media earlier reported that one of its tankers had been struck off the coast of Kharg Island.

Tehran did not immediately acknowledge attacks on US ships.

Admiral Brad Cooper, Centcom's commander, said in a statement on Saturday: "Let the message to the IRGC be clear: If you shoot at two of our ships, we will impose an even higher economic cost - taking out three of yours."

"We will not hesitate to defend American forces, and if necessary, destroy Iran's limited and exposed oil fleet."

Centcom, which oversees US military operations in the Middle East, claimed that the three Iranian oil tankers were "part of a multibillion-dollar shadow network that funds the IRGC and its regional proxies".

The strikes come nearly a week after renewed attacks between the US and Iran, which followed a period of relative calm between the warring sides.

How could US-Iran conflict end? Three experts give their views

Earlier this week, US Vice-President JD Vance said the US military was investigating Iranian claims that American strikes killed at least four people including two children at a wedding in southern Iran.

Humanitarian group the Iranian Red Crescent Society said shrapnel from a missile hit the ceremony at a home in Sirik on Tuesday, prompting Tehran to declare it a "war crime".

A 60-day ceasefire between the US and Iran formally expired last month, with little sign of a further diplomatic settlement on the horizon.

Days after the ceasefire expired, US President Donald Trump said the US would launch tougher economic measures against Iran, as well as any country that helps or does business with it.

The US and Israel first launched wide-ranging strikes on Iran on 28 February, with Iran responding by attacking Israel, US bases and allied states in the Gulf, and effectively closing the Strait of Hormuz to marine traffic.

The conflict over the strait has raised energy prices globally. And, ahead of the US midterm elections in November, Trump is facing pressure over how much the war is costing American consumers.

US and Iran trade strikes for first time in weeks

Six months into the Iran war: What has Trump accomplished?

Iran says US strike killed four at wedding in 'war crime' as US denies targeting civilians

articles.title: ESPN ripped by fans for horrific 'College GameDay' decision: 'Ruined the show!'
articles.excerpt:
Pate wants to capture the "vibe" of college campus before a big game.

The first week of college football is here, boys and girls. We've waited eight months for this day. A full slate of actual colleg...
articles.body_text:
Pate wants to capture the "vibe" of college campus before a big game.

The first week of college football is here, boys and girls. We've waited eight months for this day. A full slate of actual college football.

With all due respect to Week Zero, this is the official kickoff to the college football season. Every single team will be on the field today. We've got games from noon till midnight. The fans, the pageantry, the bands ... it's all back. Finally.

COLLEGE FOOTBALL'S FIRST FULL SATURDAY IS HERE AND IT'S A CELEBRATION OF AMERICA AT ITS BEST

Pat McAfee gestures Guns Up before ESPN's College GameDay at Texas Tech University in Lubbock, Texas, on Nov. 8, 2025. (Getty Images)

Of course, ESPN's "premiere pregame show," College GameDay, is also back. That's a big deal for college football fans. We grew up on this show. It was a Saturday morning staple during our childhoods, and now it's a staple during our kids' childhoods.

Sure, characters have changed (Lee Corso's final show was last year), but the vibe is still the same. Nothing says "fall" quite like College GameDay blaring in the living room at 9 a.m. on a crisp Saturday morning.

HOT TAKE ALERT: ESPN GETTING RID OF 'BOTTOMLINE' SCORE TICKER IS A TRAVESTY, NOT A REASON TO CELEBRATE

Now, with all that being said ... ESPN and GameDay screwed the pooch this morning by choosing to have country singer Lainey Wilson perform the show's iconic theme song — "Coming to your City" — live from Baton Rouge.

Lordy. Just awful. This has nothing to do with Wilson, by the way. I like Lainey Wilson. I'm glad ESPN at least had a country singer perform it (although it should always be Big & Rich).

But this just didn't work. The sound was off. The mic was low. You could barely understand anything Lainey was saying.

Of course, folks accused her of lip-syncing the whole thing. It was a disaster. Nothing about it worked.

Members of the Indiana dance team pose with the ESPN College GameDay bus before a college football game between the Washington Huskies and Indiana Hoosiers on Oct. 26, 2024, at Memorial Stadium in Bloomington, Ind. (Icon Sportswire via Getty Images)

I could go on and on. The internet is in lockstep on this one. No hung jury. No mistrial. No further deliberation. Everyone is on the same page.

A fan gives thumbs down during ESPN's College GameDay at Pennsylvania State University in University Park, Pa., on Sept. 27, 2025. (Getty Images)

This was a horrible decision by ESPN. Fair is fair, and I have to be fair here. It stunk. We waited eight months ... for that?

articles.title: Miss America contestant reveals surprising day job as Massachusetts police officer
articles.excerpt:
Miss Massachusetts Ashlyn Mercier reveals what inspired her law enforcement career and why competing for Miss America sends a powerful message to young girls.

Ashlyn Mercier has spent her career wear...
articles.body_text:
Miss Massachusetts Ashlyn Mercier reveals what inspired her law enforcement career and why competing for Miss America sends a powerful message to young girls.

Ashlyn Mercier has spent her career wearing a badge. Now, she's hoping to wear one of the country's most coveted tiaras.

The Westborough, Massachusetts, police officer is competing in Miss America. The final competition takes place Sept. 6 at the Palm Beach County Convention Center in West Palm Beach, Florida. Mercier is also the first police officer to be named Miss Massachusetts.

"I think there's not one single look for what a female police officer is supposed to look like," Mercier told Fox News Digital. "And if we say that there is, that's just wrong because, at the end of the day, yes, female law enforcement officers only make up approximately 14% of the force in the United States, but we don't have to look a certain way."

NAVY VETERAN TRADES MILITARY UNIFORM FOR MISS GEORGIA SASH FOLLOWING HEARTBREAKING LOSS

Ashlyn Mercier, a police officer for the town of Westborough, Massachusetts, is competing in the Miss America pageant. The final competition is taking place on Sept. 6, 2026. (Miss America)

"People are so multifaceted, women are so multifaceted, and I'm just trying to show young girls that they can chase all of their dreams simultaneously," Mercier said. "They don't have to pick one thing and make that their entire identity."

The glitzy competition dates to a 1921 beauty contest in Atlantic City, New Jersey, held a year after the 19th Amendment guaranteed women the right to vote. The organization awards scholarships and gives its titleholder a national platform for community service and advocacy.

According to the Miss America organization, more than $300,000 in tuition scholarships will provide delegates "with meaningful support as they pursue their education and continue making an impact in communities across America." (Miss America)

Mercier hopes to raise awareness of her cause, "Nick's Courage: One Smile Goes a Mile," named after her younger brother, Nicholas, a two-time pediatric cancer survivor. The initiative aims to bring positivity and hope to children battling critical illnesses.

In 2025, she took a year off from pageant competition to follow in her father's footsteps and attend the police academy.

WATCH: ACTIVE-DUTY POLICE OFFICER COMPETES IN MISS AMERICA

"I didn't know if I would ever come back and compete," Mercier said. "I was afraid of what other people would think if I chased both of those dreams at the same time. I also had this dream of becoming a police officer. But what I came to realize is that I can't worry about what other people think. I've got to focus on myself. And it ended up working out for me."

Mercier said the Westborough Police Department has been cheering her on as she balances the competition with her work as an officer. Fox News Digital reached out to the department for comment.

Ashlyn Mercier graduated from the police department in 2025. (Miss America)

"I'm really fortunate that they have been so incredibly supportive," Mercier said. "I work for an amazing department, and my co-workers have supported me 100% from the moment I told them I was competing as Miss Massachusetts to now being at Miss America. They've shown up to my sendoff parties, they've helped me with my fundraising efforts, they've sent me good luck texts."

Ashlyn Mercier told Fox News Digital that fellow female officers have been cheering her on. (Miss America)

"It's really just an honor to be surrounded by people who uplift me," she said. "It really continues to help motivate me to move forward."

Mercier said her career in law enforcement doesn't give her an advantage on the Miss America stage. She's one of the delegates representing the 50 states, the District of Columbia and Puerto Rico, each hoping to stand out.

Ashlyn Mercier started dispatching for the Westborough Fire Department. (Miss America)

GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

Ashlyn Mercier made history as the first police officer to win the state crown. (Miss America)

"I've had thousands of female law enforcement officers across the country commenting on my posts saying that they're rooting for me and that they're inspired by me," Mercier said. "There are also young girls saying that they want to get into law enforcement, and they're inspired by my story. And then, I serve my community in Westborough every single day in my capacity as a police officer, but I also get to serve my community in the role as Miss Massachusetts."

Ashlyn Mercier is highlighting Nick's Courage in honor of her younger brother. (Miss America)

"Those two things are what is so important about the Miss America opportunity," Mercier said. "Yes, we get to dress up. Yes, we get to wear pretty gowns and look beautiful. But, women's empowerment and service are the core. And if you look at it like that, you can see and draw a lot of parallels between Miss America and between my role as Officer Mercier."

Police work has also given Mercier skills she can use in the competition. She said she's comfortable communicating with different people and staying calm in nerve-wracking situations. But one challenge remains.

Ashlyn Mercier was named Miss Massachusetts 2026. (Miss America)

When asked whether getting ready for a shift or a pageant takes longer, she didn't miss a beat.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Ashlyn Mercier is a second generation police officer. (Miss America)

"Oh, absolutely getting ready for a pageant," she said with a laugh. "I do not look like this on a daily basis when I go to work. I'll have maybe some mascara on, and the hair gets slicked back in a bun. I've got that down in about two minutes flat. This definitely takes a lot longer."

PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

Ashlyn Mercier's father is a corporal with the Oxford Police Department. (Miss America)

This year's competition commemorates 105 years of Miss America. Whether she earns the title or not, Mercier said she's determined to use her platform to make a difference.

Ashlyn Mercier hopes to inspire young girls to pursue a career in law enforcement. (Miss America)

"If I do win, I just hope to be an inspiration to young women and girls looking up to [me] knowing that she can be a police officer, and she can be Miss America," Mercier said. "She can chase all her dreams at once. I've been told I should pick one, focus on one. But you can do it all. My message is to inspire the next generation."

Stephanie Nolasco is an Entertainment Reporter for Fox News Digital.

articles.title: Donna Mills does 100 sit-ups a day, plays tennis five times a week at 85 but won't quit Doritos
articles.excerpt:
The longtime Hollywood actress tells Fox News Digital how she keeps her body moving with a demanding fitness regimen.

Donna Mills is keeping fans on their toes at 85, from launching an OnlyFans accou...
articles.body_text:
The longtime Hollywood actress tells Fox News Digital how she keeps her body moving with a demanding fitness regimen.

Donna Mills is keeping fans on their toes at 85, from launching an OnlyFans account to revealing the intense fitness routine she credits with keeping her active.

The former ballerina, best known for playing the scheming Abby Cunningham on "Knots Landing," revealed to Fox News Digital the demanding fitness routine she credits with keeping her moving — including 100 sit-ups, 50 leg lifts, up to an hour on the bike and, sometimes, tennis five days a week.

And while Mills has long been disciplined about her health — including cutting out sugar — there is one indulgence she refuses to completely give up.

'KNOTS LANDING' STAR DONNA MILLS SAYS REFUSING TO POSE NUDE COST HER PLAYBOY COVER

American actress Donna Mills as she performs barre exercises in her home dance studio, Beverly Hills, California, March 18, 1983. (Bob Riha, Jr./Getty Images)

The actress revealed that nacho cheese is her flavor of choice, showing that even her disciplined wellness routine leaves room for a guilty pleasure.

"I mean, it’s not good for you. It’s not. You know, I know I shouldn’t do it," Mills admitted.

WATCH: 'Knots Landing' star Donna Mills swears by this daily routine at 85

Still, she said the popular snack has followed her throughout her decades-long career.

"Different sets that I’ve been on… for some reason, they know — they always got a bag of Doritos in the trailer for me… it’s really funny. But I’ve never lost that. I don’t eat them as much as I used to. But they’re still a treat."

Mills as she performs exercises in her home dance studio, March 18, 1983. (Getty Images)

When it comes to exercise, Mills' routine is considerably more demanding.

"I started out as a dancer, so a ballerina. I mean, I was on pointe, the whole thing," she said.

'KNOTS LANDING' STAR DONNA MILLS ISSUES URGENT WARNING ABOUT AGING

Mills said her early training instilled a work ethic that has stuck with her throughout her life.

"So that gave me a discipline that most people don’t have because ballet is very hard," she explained.

Mills starred in the TV soap opera series "Knots Landing," in June 1980. (Getty Images)

To this day, she still incorporates elements of her early training into her workouts.

DICK VAN DYKE SHOCKS FANS BY POSTING INVERSION TABLE WORKOUT AT AGE 100

"I do 100 sit-ups a day, 50 leg lifts, lots of stretching. I have a ballet barre in my little gym."

"And ride the bike for about 45 minutes or an hour," she continued.

WATCH: Donna Mills says Playboy snubbed her over nude photo refusal

She also stays active on the court whenever she can.

"I play tennis five times a week sometimes. And so that’s very, very important."

The Hollywood actress takes a similarly disciplined approach to her diet, saying a book she read years ago influenced her decision to cut back on sweets.

"I’ve always been anti-sugar," she said. "I read a book a long time ago called 'Sugar Blues' that really talked about the sugar industry and everything, and I have stayed away from it ever since."

Donna Mills stays active at 85 with daily sit-ups and tennis several times a week. (Photo by Tim P. Whitby)

Still, Mills isn't pretending her lifestyle is effortless.

"It’s a lot of stuff. You got to work at it."

'PERFECT' WORKOUT FORMULA CAN TAKE JUST 10 MINUTES A DAY, HILARIA BALDWIN SAYS

Her fitness routine comes as Mills enters what she describes as an entirely new chapter of her life.

The actress launched an OnlyFans account at 85, embracing a platform she initially knew nothing about.

WATCH: 'KNOTS LANDING' STAR DONNA MILLS TEASES 'SPICY' ONLYFANS AT 85

Mills has already seen major interest in her new venture, with Creators Inc. telling her she’s doing "incredibly well" and bringing in "many six figures" early on.

But money isn't the only draw. Mills said fans are hungry for a behind-the-scenes look at her life — something she said wasn't possible during her TV heyday.

"They want to know me. They want to know what I do during the day when I’m home. They want to see my home. They want to know much more about my personal life than we ever experienced back in the ’80s and the ’90s that, you know, the fans were cut off from."

Now, they’re "invited in" — potentially even to Mills’ vineyard.

Her OnlyFans audience has already made some unusual requests, including one involving barefoot grape-stomping.

PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

The decision also gave the Hollywood actress a chance to share never-before-seen photographs from a Playboy shoot that she says did not result in a promised cover.

Mills said she agreed to the shoot only after making it clear she would not pose nude.

"I said I would do the photo shoot for Playboy if they were okay with the fact that I wasn’t going to show anything," she recalled.

But she said the photographer continued pushing her boundaries throughout the three-day shoot. Mills insisted the photos didn't need nudity to make an impression.

The "Knots Landing" star keeps fit with 100 daily sit-ups and frequent tennis as she turns up the heat on OnlyFans. (Maureen Donaldson / Michael Ochs Archives / Getty Images; Unique Nicole / Getty Images)

GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

Now, she's bringing those images and her personality directly to fans.

"I think what the page will be, will be spicy. That’s kind of always been my thing, to be a little spicy," Mills said. "I think they’ll react to that, they’ll like that, and also it’s my chance to communicate with them through the videos and things like that and talk to them."

For Mills, the point isn't simply launching a provocative new platform. It's proving that getting older doesn't mean life gets smaller.

"When I kind of looked at it a few years ago and said, 'What do I want to do with this portion of my life, this chapter in my life?' I said, 'I’d like to be an inspiration,'" she emphasized.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

"I’d like to show people, and particularly women, that it doesn’t have to be over. It’s just a new chapter. It’s not the end... It’s just something you can enjoy. You should enjoy. It’s part of your life."

After playing one of television's most famously ambitious villains, Mills already knows exactly how Abby Cunningham would react to her latest move.

"She would say, ‘Go, girl!’ Without a doubt," Mills said. "Are you kidding? Abby would be all for it. She was for anything that was going to move her forward, that was going to be to her advantage. So, she would be dead on for this. She would love this."

Stephanie Giang-Paunon is an entertainment reporter for Fox News Digital.

articles.title: Trump negotiators Witkoff, Kushner arrive in Moscow as US pushes for end to Russia-Ukraine war
articles.excerpt: During an open to the press event in the White House's Oval Office on Friday, Sept. 4, 2026, President Donald Trump explains his decision to send special envoy Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner to Mosco...
articles.body_text:
During an open to the press event in the White House's Oval Office on Friday, Sept. 4, 2026, President Donald Trump explains his decision to send special envoy Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner to Moscow and Kyiv. Credit: Reuters.

U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff and President Donald Trump's son-in-law and adviser, Jared Kushner, are visiting Moscow and Kyiv over the weekend in an effort to end the war between Russia and Ukraine, President Donald Trump said Friday.

"We have an idea for peace," Trump told reporters on Friday. "I sent Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, two great negotiators. They've done a great job, and we sent them over to see whether or not we can get something done. And there may be a good chance that we'll do it," he said.

Ukrainian President Volodomyr Zelenskyy confirmed the news in a post on X.

"Today, it has been clearly established that U.S. envoys will be in Ukraine and Russia in the coming days. We have the details from the U.S. President’s team. We discussed today that Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner will visit Moscow and then Kyiv on Sunday. We are preparing for the visit," Zelenskyy wrote.

TRUMP ANNOUNCES SURPRISE THREE-DAY CEASEFIRE IN RUSSIA-UKRAINE WAR

Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev greets U.S. special representatives Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff upon their arrival at Vnukovo International Airport in Moscow, Russia, Sept. 5, 2026. (Reuters)

The pair will visit Russia first on Saturday and, according to Russian state-affiliated media outlet Tass, have already landed in Moscow.

They will then move on to Kyiv on Sunday, Zelenskyy confirmed. Zelenskyy also said that Ukraine will work to keep Russian airspace safe during the Americans’ visit.

CIA DIRECTOR JOHN RATCLIFFE MET WITH RUSSIAN INTELLIGENCE OFFICIALS IN VISIT TO MOSCOW, KREMLIN SAYS

Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev walks with U.S. special representatives Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff upon their arrival at Vnukovo International Airport in Moscow, Russia, Sept. 5, 2026. (Reuters)

"Just as we did during previous diplomatic visits by the American side, we will ensure the normal functioning of Russian airspace so that the negotiators can arrive safely. We are looking out for them, not for Russia. There will be no air strikes from our side, and Russia must do the same, ensuring there are no air strikes from its side for the time needed to hold these talks and handle the logistical matters related to this American visit," he wrote on X.

ZELENSKYY CONGRATULATES TRUMP ON TURNING 80 IN BIRTHDAY CALL, VOWS MORE UKRAINE PEACE TALKS AT G7 ON TUESDAY

"Our goal is to make the visit and the talks with the U.S. side as constructive and substantive as possible. We need to look for real options for how to move this war toward an end. We will see what proposals Steve and Jared bring and what they are told in Moscow in response," the Ukrainain president concluded.

Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky speaks at a press conference after meetings with the heads of the EU and Ireland, following a formal ceremony to mark the launch of Ireland's eighth EU presidency, at Dublin Castle in Dublin on July 1, 2026. (Paul Faith / AFP via Getty Images)

Zelenskyy’s Friday message came the same day that a Russian drone strike targeted the Security Service of Ukraine’s headquarters in Ukraine, Zelenskyy wrote in a public message on the app Telegram.

RUSSIA LAUNCHES BALLISTIC MISSILE ATTACK ON KYIV HOURS AFTER ZELENSKYY WARNS OF MAJOR STRIKE

Zelenskyy alleged the strike directly targeted the head of the Security Service's office.

He also wrote that he was directing the head, Oleksandr Poklad, to prepare a retaliatory strike. "I gave Poklad the task of adequately, noticeably and, if possible, mirroring the Russians' response to this attack, when everything is prepared. Our military will support this response. Glory to Ukraine!" he wrote.

PUTIN UNLEASHES NEW FURY ON UKRAINE AS REPORT EXPOSES FEAR HANGING OVER WAR’S END

At least nine people were injured in the explosion, Kyiv mayor Vitali Klitschko also wrote on Telegram.

A man looks on as smoke rises over a warehouse, which was hit by a Russian drone strike, amid Russia's attack on Ukraine, in Kyiv region, Ukraine, Aug. 27, 2026. (REUTERS/Valentyn Ogirenko/File Photo)

The visit also comes just one day after German officials formally accused Russia of attempting an explosive drone attack on a major airport in Germany.

RUSSIA’S STRIKES NEAR MOLDOVA RAISE ALARM OVER PUTIN’S PLANS FOR EUROPE’S EASTERN FLANK

"The attack on the aircraft in Leipzig was concrete; it could have triggered a catastrophe had it succeeded. The attacker was, at most, covert, but even here there is now certainty: The German government has named Russia as the mastermind. Patterns of attack, police investigations, and intelligence findings prove Russian responsibility for the drone attack," Stefan Kornelius, a spokesperson for the German federal government, wrote Friday.

Fox News Digital contacted the White House and the foreign ministries for Russia, Ukraine and Germany for further comment.

articles.body_text:
Luciano Zaccara is professor of Gulf Politics at the Qatar University Gulf Studies Center.

At the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) summit in Bishkek this week, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian received precisely the kind of political support he had hoped for. The SCO condemned the military attacks against Iran, described them as violations of international law and the UN Charter, reaffirmed Iranian sovereignty and territorial integrity, and called for the conflict to be resolved through political and diplomatic means.

But the organisation did not offer to defend Iran. That distinction between political solidarity and collective defence is important. It tells us something not only about the Iranian experience with the SCO, but about the international order that is emerging around it.

For years, discussions about multipolarity have often suggested that the US-led international system would gradually be challenged by an alternative bloc centred around China, Russia and organisations such as BRICS and the SCO. From the perspective of middle powers, joining both institutions seemed to fit neatly into this transformation. Integration into non-Western organisations was supposed to make them less vulnerable to Western isolation and pressure.

The US-Israeli war on Iran has made clear that none of these alternative relationships can produce a security guarantee comparable to those provided by formal military alliances. The lesson is not that multipolarity has failed middle powers. It is that the emerging multipolar order may work differently from what many expected.

Rather than replacing one alliance system with another, it is producing an increasingly dense network of overlapping partnerships in which states gain diplomatic and economic options without necessarily acquiring new security guarantees.

For middle powers, this may be one of the defining characteristics of the emerging order: more room for manoeuvre, but less certainty about who will stand beside them when their security is threatened.

Turkiye provides a particularly revealing example. It has been a member of NATO for more than seven decades and remains embedded in the Western security architecture. Yet Ankara has increasingly demonstrated that alliance membership does not require automatic political alignment with Washington. Turkiye has maintained relations with Russia despite the war in Ukraine, expanded its engagement with China and participated in the SCO as a dialogue partner. At the same time, its differences with the US and Israel over the future regional order in the Middle East have become increasingly visible.

This does not mean Turkiye is abandoning NATO or moving into a Chinese- or Russian-led bloc. Quite the opposite. Ankara’s strategy depends precisely on avoiding such a binary choice. Its NATO membership provides security benefits that the SCO could not replicate. Its relationships with Russia, China, Iran, the Gulf states and other regional actors, meanwhile, expand its diplomatic and economic options.

Brazil represents another good example. Unlike Turkiye, Brazil is not bound to the US through a formal military alliance. But it has traditionally operated within a US-dominated hemisphere where Washington has expected considerable political alignment from regional governments.

Brazil’s refusal to join the US-led Americas Counter-Cartel Coalition (ACCC), together with its positions on the Iran war and other recent international crises, reflects its reluctance to accept that regional proximity should translate into automatic strategic alignment.

Yet Brazil is not simply switching sides. Its participation in BRICS, its extensive economic relationship with China and its calls for reform of the international system coexist with important political and economic relations with the US and Europe. Brasília’s objective is not to exchange dependence on Washington for dependence on Beijing, but to preserve the ability to cooperate with both, and disagree with either.

This may be one of the most consequential opportunities that multipolarity offers middle powers. The rise of alternative centres of economic and political influence reduces the cost of saying no. For decades, weaker states often confronted a difficult choice when facing pressure from a dominant power: comply, resist and risk isolation, or seek protection from a rival bloc.

The proliferation of partners and institutions complicates that calculation. A government that disagrees with Washington may deepen relations with Beijing without becoming a Chinese ally. A state dependent on China economically may strengthen security ties with the US without fully aligning with Washington. Membership in BRICS does not prevent cooperation with Western institutions, just as membership in a US-led security framework does not necessarily preclude engagement with China or Russia.

India has made this logic almost an organising principle of its foreign policy. New Delhi participates in the Quad with the US, Japan and Australia while simultaneously belonging to both BRICS and the SCO. At Bishkek, India supported the SCO declaration defending Iranian sovereignty while Prime Minister Narendra Modi also stressed to Pezeshkian the importance of preserving freedom of navigation and commerce through the Strait of Hormuz.

The Gulf Cooperation Council member states are pursuing their own version of this diversification. Saudi Arabia, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates, for example, continue to depend heavily on their relationships with the US for security, while simultaneously expanding economic and diplomatic ties with China, India and other Asian powers and participating in new regional and international arrangements.

None appears eager to replace Washington with Beijing. They want relationships with both. This suggests that the most significant consequence of multipolarity for middle and smaller powers may not be the emergence of a new bloc to which they can attach themselves. It may be the declining necessity of attaching themselves exclusively to any bloc at all.

But greater autonomy comes with a cost. The same flexible arrangements that allow states to avoid choosing sides also provide fewer guarantees when crises become existential. BRICS does not have an Article 5. Neither does the SCO, which explicitly defines itself as a non-military organisation.

Strategic partnerships can provide weapons, investment, diplomatic backing and political support without obligating partners to go to war for one another.

The emerging international system is therefore unlikely to resemble a simple transition from a US-led order to a Chinese-led one, or even a confrontation between two clearly defined blocs. The older alliance system is not disappearing.

NATO remains central to European and Turkish security, while US security relationships remain indispensable across much of Asia and the Gulf. What is emerging alongside it is another layer, a more fluid landscape of overlapping institutions, selective partnerships and transactional relationships.

Multipolarity, in other words, may not require states to choose a new camp. That gives middle and smaller powers greater agency. But it also places greater responsibility for their own security upon them. The world they are entering may offer more partners, more bargaining power and more freedom to say no. What it may offer less frequently is certainty about who will say yes when they ask for protection.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

articles.title: Arizona voter-law fight reaches SCOTUS as election groups warn ‘absurd’ consequence could ensue
articles.excerpt: Federal prosecutors charge a Honduran national with voter fraud in California after he allegedly registered to vote under an alias and cast ballots in multiple elections. Fox News' Matt Finn reports o...
articles.body_text:
Federal prosecutors charge a Honduran national with voter fraud in California after he allegedly registered to vote under an alias and cast ballots in multiple elections. Fox News' Matt Finn reports on the federal indictment details, revealing the suspect received a voter registration card using a gym membership. The case highlights ongoing debates surrounding voter identification laws.

Election experts are warning the Supreme Court that affirming a lower court's ruling could mean that noncitizens, minors, or factitious people listed on state voter rolls could be impossible to remove.

The Supreme Court is set to hear oral arguments in RNC v. Mi Familia Vote this December and will determine whether a pair of Arizona's state laws which remove the registrations of noncitizen voters from voter rolls within 90 days of the election and require voters to show proof of U.S. citizenship when registering to vote are in violation of the National Voter Registration Act.

"Citizenship is a qualification for voting. If states are going to enforce that requirement, they have to be able to verify it," Justin Riemer, president & CEO of Restoring Integrity and Trust in Elections said in a statement to Fox News Digital. "And when officials find noncitizens on the voter rolls, they should be able to act before an election, not after. We are confident the Supreme Court will agree and reverse the Ninth Circuit's misguided ruling."

In an amicus brief filed on Thursday, attorneys from Center for Election Confidence, Inc., Restoring Integrity and Trust in Elections, Inc., and Honest Elections Project, argued that the Ninth Circuit Court's ruling that the Arizona laws are an act of "voter suppression" is "absurd" and raises serious threats to state rights.

FILE - Voters arrive to the polling location at the Burton Barr Central Library on November 05, 2024 in Phoenix, Arizona. RNC v. Mi Familia Vote will determine whether a pair of Arizona's state laws which remove the registrations of noncitizen voters from voter rolls within 90 days of the election and require voters to show proof of U.S. citizenship when registering to vote are in violation of the National Voter Registration Act. (Photo by Christian Petersen/Getty Images)

CLINTON-APPOINTED JUDGE TRIGGERS APPEAL AFTER BLOCKING KEY VOTER CITIZENSHIP LAW

The brief argued that Congress may regulate the mechanics of federal elections, but states have the constitutional authority to set and enforce voter qualifications — a power they argued becomes meaningless if states cannot obtain documentation needed to verify citizenship or remove people who were never eligible to register.

"Since the power to establish voting requirements is of little value without the power to enforce those requirements, it would raise serious constitutional doubts if a federal statute precluded a State from obtaining the information necessary to enforce its voter qualifications," the brief stated.

The amicus brief pushed back on the Ninth Circuit’s conclusion that Arizona cannot conduct a systematic program to remove noncitizens from voter rolls during the NVRA’s 90-day pre-election period. The federal law generally requires states to complete systematic voter-removal programs at least 90 days before a federal election, while allowing removals during that window for a voter’s request, death, criminal conviction or mental incapacity.

DEMOCRAT NEW JERSEY GOVERNOR SAYS THOUSANDS OF NONCITIZENS DISCOVERED ON VOTER ROLLS, PURGED

FILE - A volunteer picks up "Require Voter ID" sign at the press conference at the Riverside County Registrar of Voters on Monday, March 2, 2026, as GOP lawmakers gather in support of placing a voter ID measure on the November ballot. (Anjali Sharif-Paul/MediaNews Group/The Sun via Getty Images)

The groups argued that non-citizenship is not among those listed grounds because it concerns someone who was never eligible to register in the first place. They said the restriction is meant to protect eligible voters from erroneous last-minute removals — not to shield people who were never eligible to register.

"If the Ninth Circuit is right that the 90-day limitation on programs prohibits removal on these bases — because the statute has listed exceptions — States could never remove improperly registered individuals who fall within these categories, no matter when the removal happens or whether it is after a systematic inquiry," the brief said.

"Not just that, but these States could never remove these noncitizens who were never eligible to vote," the brief continued.

The brief pointed to reported registration errors in New Jersey, Illinois and Oregon as examples of why states need a mechanism to correct allegedly improper registrations. It argues that an unlawful ballot cannot be undone once cast and counted.

DHS APPROVES PLAN TO VERIFY VOTER CITIZENSHIP, MONITOR MAIL BALLOTS AS TRUMP PUSH INTENSIFIES

"American elections are for American citizens only. Period," Lisa Dixon, executive director of the Center for Election Confidence, said in a statement. "We should all support Arizona ensuring non-citizens can’t register to vote and removing any non-citizens who end up on the voter lists."

The amici also argued that the Ninth Circuit misread NVRA provisions governing what information is "necessary" for state election officials to assess a voter’s eligibility, and whether a state registration form is "equivalent" to the federal form.

FILE - Security guards stand in front of the Ninth U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals in San Francisco, Calif., on June 12, 2017. The brief argued that the Ninth Circuit wrongly concluded a voter’s citizenship attestation on a registration form is sufficient proof of eligibility. (Getty Images)

The brief argued that the Ninth Circuit wrongly concluded a voter’s citizenship attestation on a registration form is sufficient proof of eligibility and improperly interpreted an "equivalent" state form to mean one that is virtually identical to the federal form.

"Once again, far-left activists are using the courts to twist federal law into a straitjacket that prevents states from securing their elections," Jason Snead, executive director of Honest Elections Project, said in a statement to Fox News. "The Honest Elections Project urges the Supreme Court to side with Arizona and preserve the tools states need to ensure that elections are decided only by American citizens."

Elaine Mallon is a writer for Fox News Digital and Fox Business covering national politics.

articles.title: US says it hit Iran oil tankers helping finance ‘regional proxies’
articles.excerpt:
The United States military says it has struck three Iranian oil tankers after Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) launched ballistic missiles at two US Navy warships in regional waters.

U...
articles.body_text:
The United States military says it has struck three Iranian oil tankers after Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) launched ballistic missiles at two US Navy warships in regional waters.

US Central Command (CENTCOM) said a US aircraft carrier and guided-missile destroyer evaded multiple Iranian attacks on Saturday.

CENTCOM said its attack on Iranian oil carriers came after the IRGC fired ballistic missiles towards the two US warships “patrolling regional waters”. It said no personnel had been injured.

The US strikes hit Iranian oil tankers in the Gulf of Oman and near Iran’s Kharg island. The US military said it disabled two Iranian crude oil carriers and destroyed a third, targeting vessels it claims were part of a multibillion-dollar network that finances the IRGC and its “regional proxies”.

“Let the message to the IRGC be clear: If you shoot at two of our ships, we will impose an even higher economic cost – taking out three of yours,” CENTCOM commander Admiral Brad Cooper said. “We will not hesitate to defend American forces, and if necessary, destroy Iran’s limited and exposed oil fleet.”

CENTCOM did not immediately provide further details about whether the strikes on the tankers caused casualties.

The strikes come a day after US President Donald Trump said the conflict, which has resulted in the deaths of 18 US service members and a spike in global energy prices, is “small potatoes”.

Both sides have tried to inflict economic and military pain on the other, with negotiations having collapsed to end the six-month war that the US and Israel began. Almost a week ago, the US and Iran exchanged attacks after a month without direct confrontations.

articles.title: GOP lawmaker warns ActBlue 'got caught' as foreign cash probe triggers Fifth Amendment pleas
articles.excerpt:
Rep. James Comer, R-KY, joins Fox Across America With guest host Paul Mauro to provide an update on the House Oversight Committee's investigation on alleged fraud by fundraising platform ActBlue.

A t...
articles.body_text:
Rep. James Comer, R-KY, joins Fox Across America With guest host Paul Mauro to provide an update on the House Oversight Committee's investigation on alleged fraud by fundraising platform ActBlue.

A top House Republican accused Democratic fundraising powerhouse ActBlue of operating as a "money laundering operation," saying that millions of dollars in foreign contributions had flowed through the platform.

Speaking on the "Fox News Rundown" podcast, Rep. Pat Fallon, R-Texas, said ongoing congressional investigations into the group have uncovered fraud-prevention failures and noted that several people affiliated with ActBlue have invoked the Fifth Amendment while being questioned by lawmakers.

"Well, [it’s clear] ActBlue had become a money laundering operation for the Democratic Party. And that's very unfortunate," Fallon told Fox News' Jessica Rosenthal. "Their compliance and fraud prevention was severely lacking, and they actually were training their employees to do almost no verifications," he added.

TEXAS AG PAXTON SUES DEM FUNDRAISING PLATFORM ACTBLUE, ALLEGING 'FRAUDULENT AND FOREIGN DONATIONS'

Rep. Pat Fallon, R-Texas, speaks during a House Oversight and Government Reform subcommittee hearing examining the Smithsonian Institution on July 21, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)

Fallon pointed specifically to the platform's past policy of not requiring card verification value, or CVV, codes for some credit card donations, calling it a "huge red flag."

In a statement to Fox News Digital, ActBlue spokesperson De’Andra Roberts LaBoo pushed back against the GOP allegations, saying the investigation is part of a broader political attack.

"President Trump and his allies are engaged in a coordinated campaign of political retaliation and retribution against organizations that they believe threaten them — from universities and law firms to civil rights groups and philanthropies. Now, they’re working to target Democratic fundraising ahead of the midterms," Roberts LaBoo said.

"ActBlue will not be intimidated, and we refuse to slow down. No other platform does more to protect the integrity of small-dollar democracy — regardless of party. Our platform has raised a record amount of midterm-cycle contributions. With more than a million new donors, Americans are stepping up and fighting back, giving an average contribution of just $36 to the candidates and causes they believe in," she added.

DEM FUNDRAISING GIANT IN THE HOT SEAT AS GOP LAWMAKERS DEMAND ANSWERS OVER DODGED SUBPOENA

The Committee on House Administration, House Judiciary Committee and House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform are jointly investigating ActBlue's fraud-prevention practices and allegations involving illegal foreign donations.

Rep. Pat Fallon, R-Texas, arrives for Hunter Biden's deposition at the O’Neill House Office Building on Feb. 28, 2024, in Washington, D.C. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)

According to sources familiar with the matter, ActBlue co-founder Matt DeBergalis invoked the Fifth Amendment during a closed-door House deposition. ActBlue board member Kimberly Peeler-Allen also invoked the Fifth Amendment during a separate deposition.

"If they were on the up and up, then why is everyone that used to work for ActBlue taking the Fifth Amendment?" Fallon asked. "Also, why did their entire compliance team leave ActBlue after the 2024 election? I'm talking everybody. Because some shady things were going on, and they got caught with their hand in the cookie jar, and now they're running for the hills."

KEY HOUSE COMMITTEE SCHEDULES HEARING WITH EMBATTLED ACTBLUE CEO: 'NEEDS TO COME CLEAN'

In an April report, the three House committees said ActBlue's entire legal and compliance team had left the platform after the 2024 election.

"Documents produced pursuant to the Committees' subpoenas show the collapse of ActBlue's legal and compliance team in the months after the 2024 election. By March 2025, every member of ActBlue's legal and compliance team resigned, was fired, or went on extended leave from the platform," the committees wrote in April.

ACTBLUE CHIEF HEADS TO CAPITOL HILL HOT SEAT AS DONOR FRAUD PROBE INTENSIFIES

ActBlue CEO Regina Wallace-Jones prepares to testify at a Committee on House Administration hearing titled "Preventing Fraudulent Donations: Transparency, Verification, and Accountability" in Washington, D.C., on June 10, 2026. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)

ActBlue later responded to the congressional committees, disputing their findings and denying wrongdoing.

"For three years, ActBlue has been targeted by MAGA Republicans because of who we are and what we stand for, not because of any unlawful conduct. They want to undermine one of democracy’s most powerful tools because they are desperate to hold onto power," the platform said.

HOUSE DEM LASHES OUT AT GOP EFFORTS TO PROBE FOREIGN DONATIONS WITH STUNNING CLAIM ON MOTIVE

ActBlue said it has worked in "good faith" with the investigations and produced thousands of pages of materials, while accusing lawmakers of engaging in "political theater."

ActBlue said it leads the industry in preventing illegal contributions. The group said its fraud-detection system evaluates more than 140 factors and blocks contributions associated with foreign IP addresses, bank accounts and non-U.S. mailing addresses.

ACTBLUE SCRUTINY FUELS NEW GOP BILLS TO TIGHTEN ELECTION DONATION RULES

But Fallon told the "Fox News Rundown" that he believes ActBlue accepted millions of dollars in foreign contributions.

"It’s into the millions. It's hard to say right now. It is vast. And it's definitely game-changing. You can see it reflected in their fundraising numbers now. They're far down from where they were in previous election cycles," Fallon said, adding that he would welcome an investigation by the FBI or other federal agencies.

Fox News Digital’s Elizabeth Elkind and Kelly Phares contributed to this report.

Madison Colombo is a writer for Fox News Digital’s Flash, Media, and Culture team, covering daily breaking news and trending topics with an award-winning background in broadcast and digital journalism.

articles.title: Raise the Colours leader given access to Reform UK conference while on bail
articles.excerpt:
Ryan Bridge, arrested this year on suspicion of religiously and racially aggravated harassment, says party invited him

The leader of a flag campaign group who was arrested on suspicion of causing rel...
articles.body_text:
Ryan Bridge, arrested this year on suspicion of religiously and racially aggravated harassment, says party invited him

The leader of a flag campaign group who was arrested on suspicion of causing religiously and racially aggravated harassment was given access to Reform UK’s annual conference.

Ryan Bridge, whose Raise the Colours group has put up hundreds of union and St George flags across England, told the Guardian he was invited to the conference.

Raise the Colours has argued the campaign displays flags as a sign of patriotism, but it has been accused of using them to spread anti-immigrant sentiment.

Bridge’s attendance at the event comes as Reform UK has been attempting to attract more wavering centre-ground voters who have been reluctant to support the party. But a threat from its hard-right rival Restore Britain has given the party reason to pull rightwards.

At a conference event on Saturday, Nigel Farage paid tribute to the flag campaign and told Bridge personally that Reform UK would offer legal support. “What your campaign has done is wake up vast parts of this country,” Farage told Bridge from a stage inside the conference after the activist was among three people selected to ask questions of the Reform leader during a discussion hosted by Jeremy Kyle.

“If we can help you legally, we will,” said Farage, after Bridge told him he had an injunction against him putting up flags in Oxfordshire and was also facing one from Birmingham city council.

Bridge was among 10 activists who were banned from France this year after they travelled there to take part in actions intended to stop migrant boats embarking across the Channel.

He is also named along with six other people in action pursued by Birmingham city council as it seeks a high court injunction to stop activists from Raise the Colours putting flags up. The first hearing of that application will be on Tuesday.

Bridge has been on bail since Thames Valley police confirmed earlier this year that a 44-year-old male from Bromsgrove, Worcestershire, was arrested after reports of incidents of public order offences on Abingdon Road, Oxford. The force said he was arrested “on suspicion of causing racially and religiously aggravated harassment, alarm or distress” and that he had been released on police bail. Bridge denies all wrongdoing.

He is also facing a trial in East Sussex. He entered a not guilty plea at Brighton magistrates court last month after being charged with common assault in relation to an incident in the city in June and was granted bail.

Bridge told the Guardian at the Reform conference on the outskirts of Birmingham on Friday: “We have come to the event today in light of it’s in my home city of Birmingham and with what’s going on with Raise the Colours … what we are doing.”

“We got an invite, so we thought we would come along,” he added, saying he was not a member of Reform.

There are no general admission tickets to the Reform conference for members of the public. Conference attenders are almost entirely members, with the addition of some lobbyists, people with business interests, diplomatic representatives and members of the press. Commercial passes can be bought for £650 and “platinum” tickets can cost thousands.

Asked if his arrests posed a problem with him being at the event, Bridge said: “Being accused of a criminal act of raising a flag of your country in your country, I think is lesser than the actual criminal act that is going on on a daily basis from the far-left ultra NGOs.”

Reform UK did not respond when contacted about Bridge being at its conference.

His attendance was criticised by the anti-fascist campaign group Hope Not Hate, which said: “That someone as extreme as Ryan Bridge was inside the Reform conference with a pass is genuinely shocking.”

articles.title: Relatives hold cremations without bodies for Nepal’s missing flood victims
articles.excerpt: Kathmandu, Nepal – Nine days after his father, Dinesh, went missing, Sujan Achhami, 23, carries a body to the bank of the Bagmati River next to the famous Pashupatinath Temple in Nepal’s capital, Kath...
articles.body_text:
Kathmandu, Nepal – Nine days after his father, Dinesh, went missing, Sujan Achhami, 23, carries a body to the bank of the Bagmati River next to the famous Pashupatinath Temple in Nepal’s capital, Kathmandu. He lays the body on the Brahmanal – a stone on which corpses are placed for rituals. The priest reads mantras, directing Sujan to wash the body and offer a traditional clay lamp and flowers.

Catastrophic flash floods swept through northern and central Nepal on August 26, killing more than 1,200 people and leaving almost 5,000 others missing. With hopes of finding them alive – or even dead – fading, grieving relatives are being forced to say goodbye without bodies. So, many are instead performing symbolic last rites using effigies made of sacred kusha grass.

“We searched for them everywhere,” says Khim Bahadur Gharti Magar, whose uncle Tham Bahadur Pun, 71, a former British Army soldier, and aunt Chausara Pun, 64, were on a pilgrimage in northern Nepal when the flood hit. “We couldn’t find them.”

He has also performed these symbolic last rites for his missing relatives, right here on the bank of the Bagmati.

“There were 17 buses in the group they were with. During our search, we found four other people [dead bodies] who were part of the pilgrimage group. That’s why we decided to cremate,” Magar says.

Sher Bahadur Pun, the deceased man’s son-in-law and a senior health official with the Nepal government, says the family has given DNA samples to police in the hope their identities might be traced later.

For Dinesh Achhami’s family, the search for the 41-year-old has been equally devastating. A driver from Barabishe municipality in northern Nepal, Achhami was in Rasuwa – the district hit worst by the floods – at the time the surging waters barrelled down from Tibet. “We looked everywhere because we had no clear idea where he was hit,” says his uncle Raju Achhami.

Maniram Tharu narrowly survived the flood while working at the Upper Trishuli 1 hydropower project. His 30-year-old brother Dipendra – also a hydropower worker who was employed in a different, downstream project – and sister-in-law Phool Maya Tamang, in her 40s, have been missing since the flood.

“I cannot find their names on the list of those reported safe,” he says. “We don’t know where to go, what to do. We are worried. They have small children who are safe because they are living with other family members.”

The scale of the disaster has overwhelmed the authorities. Nepal Police spokesman Abi Narayan Kafle says storing recovered bodies remains a major challenge.

“The proper way would have been to preserve bodies until identification is established but we are not in that condition,” he says. “Many bodies are already in very bad shape, decomposed, some even in pieces, and cannot be preserved for extended periods.”

So authorities are temporarily burying unidentified bodies – with the aim of exhuming them and handing them to relatives once their identities are established.

Out of 1,344 bodies recovered so far, a total of 1,030 bodies have been buried in this way. Just 96 bodies have been handed over, after being identified by families, authorities say.

According to Kafle, the bodies have been properly numbered and have been buried at various sites in Chitwan, Nuwakot, Rasuwa, Kathmandu, Pokhara and other regions of Nepal.

But, he said, police have collected DNA samples from all bodies found so far before their burial, “to enable identification and matching with families later”.

Many in Nepal have been outraged by the government ‘s decision to carry out mass temporary burials of the deceased, describing it as going against Hindu religious traditions.

At the bank of the Bagmati next to Pashupatinath Temple, a veteran priest tells Al Jazeera that the past two days have been among the busiest he has witnessed since the 2015 earthquake, in which nearly 9,000 people died. Then, he said, most families “at least had bodies” to cremate.

As Nepal deals with its latest humanitarian crisis, the priest is this time helping carry out the symbolic cremations. He says they’re legitimate, according to Hindu scriptures. But that families are having to perform symbolic rituals is still a tragedy, he says.

articles.title: US envoys arrive in Moscow ahead of Ukraine talks
articles.excerpt:
Steve Witkoff (left) and Jared Kushner (right) are due to travel to Kyiv after talks in Moscow

Two of US President Donald Trump's top envoys have arrived in Moscow ahead of a weekend of talks aimed a...
articles.body_text:
Steve Witkoff (left) and Jared Kushner (right) are due to travel to Kyiv after talks in Moscow

Two of US President Donald Trump's top envoys have arrived in Moscow ahead of a weekend of talks aimed at accelerating efforts to end the war in Ukraine.

Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner were due in the Russian capital on Saturday, where they will hold talks before travelling to Kyiv on Sunday for discussions with Ukraine.

Trump told reporters on Friday the pair were "bringing with them a proposal to end the war". So far, efforts from the US and its allies to broker a peace deal have failed to deliver a breakthrough.

US news outlet Axios reported the US envoys would separately meet both Russian President Vladimir Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky.

Witkoff and Kushner were pictured being greeted by Russian diplomat Kirill Dmitriev after landing at Moscow's Vnukovo Airport.

Flight tracking data showed a US government plane had travelled from Helsinki, Finland, where it flown to from the US earlier in the day.

Steve Witkoff (left) next to Jared Kushner (centre) as they are greeted by Russia's Kirill Dmitriev

The two envoys have travelled to Moscow on multiple occasions since Trump returned to office, but Sunday would be their first visit to Kyiv. Delegations from Ukraine have attended talks in the US over the past 18 months.

Russian state media, citing the Kremlin, reported that Putin had ordered no strikes on Kyiv for three days, starting at midnight tonight, due to the US visit.

Earlier on Saturday, Zelensky said Russia had fired "demonstrative" strikes on airports in Kyiv and Boryspil overnight ahead of his planned meeting with the US.

Ukraine's president added: "Clearly, these Russian strikes on the airports are a reaction to the discussions and preparations for the possibility of the US side using an aircraft to travel to Ukraine and land at Kyiv Airport or Boryspil Airport."

Ukraine's airspace has been closed since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022.

Zelensky said on Friday he would guarantee the safety of Russian airspace during the envoys' visit and called for Russia to do the same for Ukraine.

He also said an overnight Russian strike on a civilian building in the Dnipro region killed four people and injured five others.

Witkoff and Kushner's visit to Moscow comes just over a week after a rare visit to the Russian capital by the head of the CIA, John Ratcliffe.

There was no official comment from Washington or the Kremlin on what was discussed. Speaking last week, Trump described the meeting as "semi-routine".

Last year, the US, Ukraine and Russia separately suggested that a deal to end the war was edging closer following a flurry of talks brokered by the Americans.

European allies also held talks in Paris but discussions ultimately ended without a breakthrough. Key disagreements remain between the warring sides on issues such as territory and security guarantees for Ukraine.

In recent months, both Russia and Ukraine have intensified their aerial attacks as fighting continues.

Ukraine said it has struggled to repel attacks due to a lack of interceptor missiles, while Kyiv has focused its strikes on Russian economic infrastructure targets.
