articles.body_text:
Fox News Flash top entertainment and celebrity headlines are here.

President Trump boasted about progress made with one of his Hollywood Special Ambassadors, Jon Voight.

The commander-in-chief admitted he had a "great and very interesting meeting" with the "movie legend," who he appointed to a special envoy in 2025 which includes Mel Gibson and Sylvester Stallone.

"He is a fantastic man who loves our Country, and feels strongly about the Motion Picture and Television Industry," Trump shared on his Truth Social platform.

MEL GIBSON APOLOGIZES FOR MOCKING ASL INTERPRETER, BLAMES 'SPONTANEOUS THOUGHTLESS IDIOCY'

Donald Trump has a longtime friend in actor Jon Voight, who he appointed as a special ambassador to Hollywood in 2025. (Mandel Ngan)

"He hates what’s happened to it! It is being dissipated in its entirety. It has moved to Canada, and other Countries, with very little work being done anymore in the United States."

Trump continued, "Hollywood is a Complete and Total Disaster! Despite the name, it is getting very little work. There is no incentive to be there, and it is hurting California very badly."

TRUMP NAMES SYLVESTER STALLONE, MEL GIBSON AND JON VOIGHT AS SPECIAL AMBASSADORS TO 'VERY TROUBLED' HOLLYWOOD

The president noted that Jon, along with industry leaders, suggested a federal tax incentive in order to "Make our Movie and Television Production Business GREAT AGAIN, perhaps GREATER THAN EVER BEFORE!"

"The amount of money spent on Tax Incentives will be made up tenfold by the money pouring into the Treasury’s coffers," Trump wrote. "Meetings are being set up with the Leaders of both Parties in order to get this done. It should be Bipartisan, especially since so much money is being lost in California, and other largely Blue States.

"I am going to suggest that Republicans and Democrats get together, and immediately craft Legislation to save the Movie, Television, and Entertainment Business in America. Congress should approve, immediately, a Federal Production Incentive to create Entertainment Jobs in America."

Jon Voight proposed a detailed plan in May 2025 to President Donald Trump to "Make Hollywood Great Again." (Steven Paul)

He added, "It can be done quickly, accurately, efficiently and, importantly, will benefit ALL of America. What we watch on the Silver Screen should be made in what was once the Movie and Motion Picture Capital of the World. Let’s get this done!"

Voight's representatives did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Motion Picture Association Chairman and CEO Charles Rivkin welcomed the proposal from Trump.

"For over a century, American studios, casts, and crews have produced the films and series that the world wants to see," he said in a statement shared with Fox News Digital. "A federal incentive would be a landmark step toward bringing more production to local communities in all 50 states, strengthening our nation’s economy, and making our country a more competitive place to produce, create, and tell great stories."

Rivkin added, "We applaud President Trump’s support for this vital action, and we look forward to continuing to work with the White House and bipartisan leaders in Congress to enact a meaningful and effective national incentive into law."

Shortly before Inauguration Day for his second term in office, Trump revealed the Special Ambassadors program in efforts to promote business in Hollywood.

Trump appointed Sylvestor Stallone, Jon Voight, and Mel Gibson to his special ambassadors program last year. (Getty Images)

"It is my honor to announce Jon Voight, Mel Gibson, and Sylvester Stallone, to be Special Ambassadors to a great but very troubled place, Hollywood, California," Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform.

"They will serve as Special Envoys to me for the purpose of bringing Hollywood, which has lost much business over the last four years to Foreign Countries, BACK—BIGGER, BETTER, AND STRONGER THAN EVER BEFORE!"

He added, "These three very talented people will be my eyes and ears, and I will get done what they suggest. It will again be, like The United States of America itself, The Golden Age of Hollywood!"

In May 2025, Voight, along with special advisor Steven Paul, submitted a "comprehensive plan" to the president to save the film and television industry.

GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

Voight and Paul met with "dozens of leading film and television organizations (guilds, unions, studios and streamers) about what changes need to be made to increase domestic film production," according to a statement.

Jon Voight spoke before then President-elect Donald Trump arrived at a rally ahead of his Inauguration. (Elizabeth Frantz/Reuters)

PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

The meeting was conducted in person with Trump at his Mar-a-Lago residence in Florida and included SP Media Group/Atlas Comics President Scott Karol.

"The proposal includes federal tax incentives, significant changes to several tax codes, the establishment of co-production treaties with foreign countries, and infrastructure subsidies for theater owners, film and television production companies, and post-production companies," the statement said. "The proposal also includes a focus on job training, and tariffs in certain limited circumstances."

He added, "This plan is about leveling the playing field so that producing right here in America is not only a competitive option, but the first choice."

Jon Voight attended the Commander in Chief Ball at the inauguration of Donald Trump. (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)

The White House and its relevant policy advisors were in the process of reviewing the proposal.

"While President Trump regularly corresponds with his Hollywood Ambassadors, including Jon Voight, to restore America’s cultural dominance, it was President Trump himself who formulated the idea of using tariffs to Make Hollywood Great Again," White House Spokesman Kush Desai told Fox News Digital at the time.

Tracy Wright is an entertainment reporter for Fox News Digital. Send story tips to Tracy.Wright@fox.com.

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email, fr...
articles.body_text:
‘Opera House of the west’ still slated to open to the public as scheduled on 7 November, NSW arts minister says

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

An investigation is under way into allegations of misconduct involving senior executives at the soon-to-be-opened Powerhouse Parramatta.

The $915m museum in western Sydney, billed as one of the world’s most significant new museum projects, is set to open in November.

On Thursday, the Powerhouse chief executive, Lisa Havilah, stood aside, pending the investigation of fresh allegations regarding governance and procurement at the museum, the New South Wales government announced.

Allegations had been put to several Powerhouse executives as part of a misconduct investigation ahead of the institution’s formal opening, the NSW arts minister, John Graham, confirmed at a budget estimates hearing on Monday.

“The idea that two of the senior executives were working through this process, this detailed process, and could also make sure that went smoothly was really starting to become unsustainable,” he said.

The museum’s chief operating officer, Mark Wilsdon, is on leave and is providing significant information as part of the investigation, Graham said.

Havilah agreed to step aside following a conversation about further allegations that had come to light, the department of creative industries secretary, Melanie Hawyes, told the hearing.

But she cautioned any interim leadership arrangement should not be interpreted as a sanction or finding.

“These allegations that have come to light need to be tested, and that is what this investigation will do,” said Hawyes.

NSW government architect Abbie Galvin has been appointed interim chief executive and former Opera House chief executive Louise Herron has been appointed as a strategic advisor, with both to start their roles on Tuesday.

A separate NSW Treasury review of the museum’s operational budget is separate to any allegations, Hawyes said.

Spending at the Powerhouse under Havilah’s leadership has included items such as a documentary on the building of the institution, to cost at least $1.7m, about $5m on marketing, and $333,500 on the interior design of on-site accommodation.

In response to a whistleblower complaint, an initial investigation was launched in March 2025 and the state’s anti-corruption commission was notified, while a formal misconduct investigation began last December.

The procurement deals in question were under about $6m, the amount the chief executive is authorised to spend without ministerial approval, the hearing was told.

Graham defended his handling of the controversial project, insisting that issues going back to at least 2023 had been dealt with appropriately.

The Powerhouse board members including chair of trustees David Borger were not subject to the the allegations, and the board’s audit committee has assisted with investigations, Graham confirmed.

The minister said he was confident the project, which he described as the Opera House of the west, would open to the public as scheduled on 7 November.

articles.body_text:
United States Army Secretary Daniel Driscoll has submitted his resignation following months of tension with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, according to media reports.

Asked about a Wall Street Journal report on Driscoll’s resignation on Monday, the White House did not deny it.

“Secretary Driscoll has been highly effective in advancing President Trump’s agenda to Make America Strong Again at the Department of the Army by providing outstanding leadership during historic military operations, restoring an emphasis on readiness and lethality, assisting with negotiations between Russia and Ukraine, and more,” Spokeswoman Anna Kelly said in a statement.

“The United States Army is more powerful than ever thanks to his work alongside the Commander-in-Chief and Secretary of War,” she added.

The Reuters news agency, citing a source familiar with the matter, said it was unclear whether the White House has accepted Driscoll’s resignation.

Driscoll, who is considered close to Vice President JD Vance, is the latest senior official to leave the Pentagon under Hegseth.

The defence secretary fired Army Chief of Staff Randy George in April, while the Army’s commander in Europe and Africa, General Christopher Donahue, unexpectedly stepped down in June.

Hegseth has removed several other generals and admirals, including the head of the Navy.

The Pentagon abruptly announced in April that Navy Secretary John Phelan was leaving the job, becoming the first head of a military service to depart during US President Donald Trump’s second term.

Democratic Michigan U.S. Senate candidate ...
articles.body_text:
Michigan Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed responded to reports of his past controversial comments and deleted videos on "The Breakfast Club."

Democratic Michigan U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed defended his past controversial comments about Fourth of July fireworks during a radio appearance Monday.

While appearing on "The Breakfast Club," El-Sayed was asked by host Charlamagne tha God about his previous support for defunding the police and criticism of firework celebrations on Independence Day. El-Sayed pushed back against the criticism.

"They're coming at me on fireworks," El-Sayed said. "I'm like, 'All right, first, if your whole conception of America is that it's fireworks, I'm so sorry. You don't have a complete conception of America. But even then, right, like what is it?'"

WASHINGTON POST THROWS COLD WATER ON DC FIREWORKS WITH REPORT OF ‘HAZARDOUS AIR POLLUTION’

CNN reported that Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate Abdul El-Sayed deleted approximately 100 YouTube videos before launching his campaign. (The Washington Post via Getty Im)

He continued: "I said, 'Well, every time we do a fireworks show, it destroys the air quality and people have asthma exacerbations and heart attacks the next day.' That's all I was saying. You know what I mean? I'm not saying we shouldn't have fireworks. I'm just saying maybe like there are other ways to show your love."

El-Sayed's comments follow a CNN report earlier this month that revealed that El-Sayed deleted or hid approximately 100 YouTube videos before launching his Senate campaign. Among them included a plea that Americans "please" find another way to celebrate the Fourth of July besides using fireworks, citing air quality and the risks to children and pets as reasons.

SOCIALIST CANDIDATES CAN DELETE OLD POSTS, BUT THEY CAN'T ERASE THEIR RADICALISM

The video allegedly included four reasons "why fireworks suck" and a chapter titled "Fireworks just aren't worth it: hear us out."

Democratic candidate for U.S. Senate Abdul El-Sayed previously featured in a video allegedly explaining why fireworks "suck." (Scott Olson/Getty Images)

While appearing on "Hannity" earlier this month, Republican nominee Mike Rogers called out El-Sayed for his deleted posts and comments.

ABDUL EL-SAYED PLAYS DOWN HASAN PIKER TIES AFTER STREAMER’S VIRAL ANTISEMITISM FIRESTORM

"This guy spent hours hating on what most Michiganders would enjoy in their pastimes, and he should be held to account for that," Rogers said. "These are views that he held, that he was pretty strong about, but he knew that he had to delete them all… If people really knew who he was, they wouldn’t vote for him."

Republican Senate nominee Mike Rogers has called out Abdul El-Sayed for his past comments. (Sarah Rice/Getty Images ; Jeff Kowalsky/ AFP via Getty Images)

Fox News Digital reached out to the El-Sayed and Rogers campaigns for comment but did not immediately receive a response.

Lindsay Kornick is an associate editor for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to lindsay.kornick@fox.com and on Twitter: @lmkornick.

CNN anchor Wolf Blitzer issued a mea culpa Monday after he...
articles.body_text:
CNN anchor Wolf Blitzer issued a mea culpa after making a false suggestion about President Donald Trump's executive order on mail-in voting.

CNN anchor Wolf Blitzer issued a mea culpa Monday after he falsely suggested U.S. troops abroad would be impacted by the Trump administration's crackdown on mail-in voting.

On Friday's installment of "The Situation Room," Blitzer sat down with Democratic Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger to discuss the lawsuit the commonwealth filed alongside other blue states to block President Donald Trump's executive order from March to curb mail-in voting, which was slapped with a 14-day temporary restraining order last week by a federal judge.

"The continued attacks that we're seeing from the Trump administration is really just an effort to get people fearful, to get people to stay home, and, in many cases, to eliminate what is a valid, safe, secure way for people to be able to have their voices heard and to vote," Spanberger said.

CNN APOLOGIZES AFTER MISTAKENLY AIRING IMAGE OF DOLLY PARTON IMPERSONATOR DURING REPORT ON ICON'S DEATH

President Donald Trump displays a signed executive order curbing mail-in voting in the Oval Office of the White House in Washington, D.C., on Tuesday, March 31, 2026. (Aaron Schwartz/CNP/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

"And in Virginia, you have a lot of military personnel who totally rely on mail-in ballots if they want to be able to express their opinions," Blitzer told the governor.

"That's true," Spanberger replied. "It's members of the military service, of our diplomatic service, intelligence services, people serving overseas in service to our country who get their ballots mailed to them at the various postings throughout the world."

FEDERAL JUDGE AGAIN BLOCKS TRUMP'S MAIL BALLOT ORDER JUST BEFORE MIDTERMS

Democratic Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger falsely claimed U.S. troops overseas would be impacted by Trump's crackdown on mail-in voting. (Graeme Sloan/Bloomberg/Getty Images)

However, Blitzer made a "quick note of clarification" at the end of Monday's program in reference to his exchange with Spanberger.

"We discussed legal challenges to the Trump administration’s directives for the Postal Service on mail-in voting. A comment I made suggested that U.S. military and overseas voters' ballots would be impacted by these directives. I want to be clear right now: those ballots are exempt from the Postal Service’s new rules implementing the president’s March executive order," Blitzer told viewers.

"Those groups are covered under the Uniformed and Overseas Absentee Voting Act, just to be specific on that point," he added.

CLICK HERE FOR THE LATEST MEDIA AND CULTURE NEWS

CNN anchor Wolf Blitzer issued a "quick note of clarification" after falsely suggesting U.S. troops would be impacted by Trump's executive order cracking down on mail-in ballots. (Kristina Bumphrey/Variety via Getty Images)

A spokesperson for CNN pointed to Blitzer's comments and declined to comment further.

Joseph A. Wulfsohn is a media reporter for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to joseph.wulfsohn@fox.com and on Twitter: @JosephWulfsohn.

articles.title: US army secretary Dan Driscoll resigns over reported friction with Pete Hegseth
articles.excerpt:
Resignation comes after months of turmoil at Pentagon, from leaked investigation to ousting of senior officials

Army secretary Dan Driscoll has handed his resignation to Donald Trump, the White House...
articles.body_text:
Resignation comes after months of turmoil at Pentagon, from leaked investigation to ousting of senior officials

Army secretary Dan Driscoll has handed his resignation to Donald Trump, the White House said on Monday, becoming the latest high-profile figure to depart the defense department.

The army official, who is second in line to defense secretary Pete Hegseth, had reportedly been eyeing an exit from the Pentagon amid apparent friction with the secretary.

“Secretary Driscoll has been highly effective in advancing President Trump’s agenda to Make America Strong Again at the Department of the Army by providing outstanding leadership during historic military operations, restoring an emphasis on readiness and lethality, assisting with negotiations between Russia and Ukraine, and more,” White House spokesperson Anna Kelly said in a statement to the Associated Press.

“The United States Army is more powerful than ever thanks to his work alongside the Commander-in-Chief and Secretary of War,” she added.

The news was first reported by the Wall Street Journal.

The resignation comes after months of turmoil at the defense department, which has seen numerous incidents, from leak investigations and budget issues to the ousting of several senior officials including the army chief of staff Randy George in April. In June, the army’s commander of its forces in Europe and Africa, Gen Christopher Donahue, unexpectedly stepped down.

Driscoll was a George ally, and lamented his departure, as did Republican and Democratic lawmakers. Driscoll told Congress in April that he and his family drove to George’s house following his resignation “and we all gave him a hug”.

“That being said, the civilian leadership, the design of our system, is that they get to pick the leaders that they want,” Driscoll added.

Driscoll is an Iraq war veteran, tech investor and former adviser to JD Vance, whom Driscoll met at Yale law school. When nominating Driscoll in 2024, Trump called him “a disruptor and change agent”.

As army secretary, Driscoll was tapped for the unusual role of key negotiator to try to end the war between Russia and Ukraine. He was also a major force behind trying to cut the red tape for military contractors to quickly develop more drones and counter-drone capabilities as warfare rapidly changes around the world.

The Senate confirmed him in February 2025, voting 66-28, following an armed services committee hearing that was largely non-confrontational and focused on how the army could modernize its systems, improve recruiting and beef up the military industrial base.

articles.title: Tensions erupt in House hearing as GOP advances anti-socialism resolution while Dems rage: 'Silly season'
articles.excerpt:
House GOP Conference Chairwoman Lisa McClain spoke with Fox News Digital about the fight against socialists and a pair of votes in Congress to test House Democrats' resolve.

House Republicans are tee...
articles.body_text:
House GOP Conference Chairwoman Lisa McClain spoke with Fox News Digital about the fight against socialists and a pair of votes in Congress to test House Democrats' resolve.

House Republicans are teeing up a pair of bills this week to put Democrats on the record about where they stand on their party's socialist insurgency.

The House Rules Committee just advanced a resolution to condemn socialism during its Monday meeting, with no Democrats voting in favor of moving it forward. Democrats, in fact, criticized the resolution as a waste of time.

Rep. Jim McGovern, D-Mass., called the bill "nonsense" and argued it did little to better the lives of Americans.

"So you're concerned about rising gas, or are you concerned about grocery prices? You know, don't worry. Republicans in Congress are passing another non-binding resolution condemning socialism," McGovern said.

HOUSE REPUBLICAN AIMS TO PUT DEMOCRATS ON THE RECORD OVER DSA WITH RESOLUTION CONDEMNING SOCIALISM

Speaker of the House Mike Johnson, R-La., and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., attend the U.S. Holocaust Memorial Museum's National Commemoration of the Days of Remembrance ceremony in Emancipation Hall on Tuesday, April 14, 2026. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc. via Getty Images)

Tensions erupted at one point as Rep. Joe Neguse, D-Colo., clashed with Committee on House Administration Chairman Bryan Steil, R-Wis., over the definition of socialism.

Neguse had attempted to press Steil on whether he would see President Donald Trump trying to take a "20% stake" in Kroger grocery stores as socialism, to which Steil replied he would "want to see the details."

"Oh, you'd want to see the details," Neguse yelled as the two men spoke over each other. "You said if the government owns grocery stores, that would be socialist. But if, of course, Donald Trump were to announce an equity stake in a grocery store, well, 'I'd have to really see the details,' because we all know the play."

Steil said he would be open to seeing such a proposal if it had a national security imperative, but stated repeatedly that Neguse was posing a hypothetical.

At one point, Rules Committee Chairwoman Virginia Foxx, R-N.C., chided Neguse for interrupting Steil.

Steil shot back at one point, "Some folks on your side of the aisle would like to have government-run grocery stores. I think that's nuts."

"And if the president of the United States announced that the United States government was taking an...equity stake in grocery stores?" Neguse pressed.

Rep. Bryan Steil sits at a Trump rally in Wisconsin. (Jim Vondruska/Getty Images)

After more back-and-forth, Steil said, "I think there would need to be a national security rationale for the action. I don't see any in your hypothetical. I don't see a national security focus."

Neguse called it a "helpful answer," to which Steil quipped, "It's a hypotherical. So we're entering silly season."

A House-wide test known as a "rule vote" on the resolution will take place on Tuesday afternoon, followed finally by a vote on the resolution itself on Tuesday evening, according to a provisional schedule obtained by Fox News Digital.

SOCIALISM SURGES AMONG DEMOCRATS AS PARTY LEADERS REJECT DSA AGENDA: ‘PACK OF FOOLS’

It's not uncommon for Democrats on the House Rules Committee to oppose GOP-led measures. But the move is especially stark as Republicans seize on the left's inter-party civil war that has dominated the midterm election cycle.

Republicans are capitalizing on that civil war with another measure expected for a vote on Wednesday afternoon, according to that provisional schedule. That vote will be on a constitutional amendment to cap the number of Supreme Court justices at nine.

DEMOCRATIC SENATOR CLAIMS GOP 'STOLE' TWO SCOTUS SEATS IN 2016, 2020, CALLS FOR EXPANSION

Several top progressives, including former Vice President Kamala Harris and Sens. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., and Ed Markey, D-Mass., have called for expanding the Supreme Court to up to 13 seats.

House GOP leaders have opted to fast-track that legislation past the House Rules Committee. In exchange, however, it will need two-thirds of the chamber to pass as opposed to a simple majority.

CARVILLE UNLOADS ON DSA SOCIALISTS: 'DON'T USE OUR GOD---- NAME'

"It's time for the Democrats to pick a side. Stop playing the middle. Be proud of who you are. You were elected to lead, so lead. Have an opinion. We intend to put you on record," House GOP Conference Chair Lisa McClain, R-Mich., told Fox News Digital.

Chairwoman Lisa McClain Hosts "A Warning to America: Stories from Survivors of Communism" Roundtable. (Courtesy of House Republican Conference)

"Do you want to pack the Supreme Court or not? It's really simple. It's a yes or no vote. It's no bigger than that. Two — do you believe in socialism? If you do, you should say it loud and say it proud. I personally don't believe in socialism. I like the fact that we have a democracy, that we a republic, that we have a free society. And I'm proud to put myself on record."

Meanwhile the top Democrat, House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., side-stepped a question on whether he supports the anti-socialism resolution on Monday.

"I haven't taken a look at that resolution, although it's my understanding that the resolution elevates the so-called SAVE America Act, which is just the 'Suppress the Vote Act.' And I'm not clear how many Democrats are actually gonna support a resolution whose focus is on trying to rig the midterm election by elevating this voter suppression legislation that Donald Trump has been trying to jam down the road to the American people for the last year," he told reporters.

JOHNSON SCORES COMMANDING VICTORY IN FIGHT TO RAM SAVE AMERICA ACT THROUGH DEMOCRAT OPPOSITION

In addition to condemning socialism, the resolution also hails Republican-led election security bills as "common-sense election integrity measures, including proof of citizenship, photo identification, and database checks."

It calls for the "enforcement" of the Safeguarding American Voter Eligibility (SAVE) Act, which has passed the House but has not been taken up in the Senate.

Democrats have largely panned that legislation as attempts at voter suppression.

Rep. Mary Gay Scanlon, D-Pa., said the bill was a bid to "silence political opponents."

Members of the Democratic Socialists of America gather outside a Trump-owned building on May Day, May 1, 2019, in New York City. (Getty Images)

"Let's scare people with yet another boogeyman and not do anything about it. Not really solve problems, just try to scare people," Scanlon said.

Meanwhile, Rep. Nick Langworthy, R-N.Y., pointed out that Democratic socialists were already in power in his own state and warned it could spread elsewhere.

"I've seen firsthand the alarming rise of socialism...families in western New York have watched one-party rule in Albany pile on more taxes, more mandates, more government control, while hardworking taxpayers are left to foot the bill," Langworthy said. "And now downstate, we've watched the socialist left move more from the activist fringe into positions of real, serious political power. And anyone thinks that these ideas are going to stay confined in New York City is sadly mistaken."

articles.title: Rising microplastics in soil a threat to UK food security, MPs and campaigners say
articles.excerpt:
Report calls for legally binding targets to cut microplastic pollution as soil ‘is a complex living ecosystem’

The accumulation of microplastics in soil presents an emerging threat to the UK’s food s...
articles.body_text:
Report calls for legally binding targets to cut microplastic pollution as soil ‘is a complex living ecosystem’

The accumulation of microplastics in soil presents an emerging threat to the UK’s food security, according to scientists, MPs and campaigners who have called for legally binding targets to cut microplastic pollution.

UK agricultural soils have been identified as among the most contaminated by microplastics in Europe, often as a result of repeated applications of sludge from water treatment works as fertiliser, according to a report published by the all-party parliamentary group (APPG) on microplastics.

With extreme weather caused by climate breakdown already placing new pressures on agriculture, protecting soil from additional and unknown pressures is becoming increasingly important, it argues.

Alberto Costa, the MP for South Leicestershire and chair of the APPG, said: “Despite the evidence, the UK’s response remains limited. Existing measures tackle only a tiny proportion of microplastic emissions. We urgently need a preventative approach focused on reducing microplastic releases at source to protect human health and food security.”

Prof Cressida Bowyer, the director of the Revolution Plastics Institute at the University of Portsmouth, was the senior author on the report, produced in collaboration with the APPG and the Women’s Institute. The report follows up an earlier collaboration that focused on plastic microfibres from synthetic textiles.

Microplastics are pieces of plastic between 1 micrometre and 5 millimetres in size. They are often shed by the breakdown of everyday plastic items such as synthetic textiles, packaging, paints, cosmetics or car tyres.

Nanoplastics are particles smaller than 1 micrometre, which makes them small enough to permeate through biological membranes. “Everywhere we look, we find them,” Bowyer said. “Doesn’t matter how deep, how high, how obscure the sampling site, we will find microplastics. And similarly we’re finding microplastics now throughout the human body.”

She added: “We’re starting to realise that our exposure to microplastics is happening across the whole of the plastics lifecycle. So not just during the production phase and at the disposal end, where most people think of microplastics contamination occurring. But also during our use of plastic, when we’re using plastic packaging or when we’re wrapping ourselves in that lovely soft, cosy blanket on the sofa, or chopping our mushrooms on that plastic chopping board.”

Submissions of evidence to the report showed particular concerns around the presence of microplastics in soil, which Bowyer said “impacts the biological, the chemical and the physical functioning of the soil and the soil fertility itself”.

According to Bowyer, plastic particles affect the soil structure, changing the water capacity of soil; they affect the microbial community, the bacteria and fungi that are crucial to soil health; and they affect the soil fauna, with earthworms ingesting microplastics undergoing physiological changes.

She said it was important to remember that “soil is not an inert material. It’s a complex living ecosystem; it’s very finely balanced. [It is a] complex ecosystem that supports the growth of crops that feed us. The second thing to remember that’s really important is that microplastics, they’re not just polymer particles … they’re basically chemical cocktails.”

There are more than 16,000 chemicals used in plastics. About 4,000 are known to be harmful to health, while most of the rest have never undergone safety testing, the report notes.

“Microplastics can also pick up from the environment further contaminants,” Bowyer said. “So they become like sponges or magnets for other things like bacteria, heavy metals, viral particles, other chemicals.”

The report makes five policy recommendations: legally binding targets for cutting microplastic pollution, regulation of the largest sources of microplastic releases, extended producer responsibility to reduce releases across the plastics lifecycle, improved wastewater, sewage sludge and soil protections, and a coordinated national monitoring and evidence system to oversee the issue.

The report’s co-author Dr Antaya March, the director of the Revolution Plastics Institute’s Global Plastics Policy Centre, said: “The UK has an opportunity to move from a fragmented response to a coordinated strategy that tackles microplastics across the plastics lifecycle. We should not wait for every scientific uncertainty to be resolved before acting where the evidence already shows that intervention can prevent pollution and reduce future risks.”

The Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs was contacted for comment.

articles.title: UK houses near top state secondary schools cost £40,000 more, research reveals
articles.excerpt:
Premium of nearly 10% paid by housebuyers comparable with cost of a cheaper private school over seven years

A house near a top state secondary school costs an extra £40,000 on average, according to r...
articles.body_text:
Premium of nearly 10% paid by housebuyers comparable with cost of a cheaper private school over seven years

A house near a top state secondary school costs an extra £40,000 on average, according to research that reveals education premiums that rank alongside some private school fees.

The average property in a postcode district that includes a top 50 state secondary commands a price tag of £415,791, compared with £375,217 across the wider local authority areas in which those schools are located, a UK-wide analysis by the estate agent Yopa found.

The £40,574 extra, a premium of about 11%, can be compared with an average annual fee of £23,000 charged by private schools, according to the Good Schools Guide.

However, some charge less than £6,000 a year, indicating that over seven years of secondary education parents could end up paying a similar sum to the average extra cost of a house near a top state school.

The increased price tag for such properties varies significantly across the country, according to the research, although individual cases can be less informative than the overall average, due to local market factors.

Bishop Vesey’s grammar school in the well-to-do West Midlands town of Sutton Coldfield tops the table of schools where buyers are likely to pay much more than in the surrounding area.

Homes across the B74 postcode district go for an average of £509,964, a premium of £275,814 compared with the average of £234,150 in Birmingham, which includes more economically deprived areas.

In London, the biggest premium is paid by people living close to Henrietta Barnett school, a grammar academy for girls. The average property across its NW11 postcode is valued at 37% more than in the rest of the surrounding borough of Barnet, equivalent to an additional £354,288.

However, there are some outliers to the trend. Across the postcode district home to Reading school and Kendrick school, the average property costs £276,870. That is £84,373 below the wider Reading average of £361,243.

Verona Frankish, the chief executive of Yopa, said: “For many homebuyers with children, the quality of local schools is one of the most important considerations when deciding where to live and, with the new school year approaching, education will be front of mind for many families considering their next move.”

Separate research reveals that in London, homebuyers with children who go to a nearby private school are opting in to a double whammy of extra costs, with properties near a top fee-paying establishment – which are often located in the most upmarket areas – going for premiums of up to 77%.

Queen’s college, London, tops the table. Homes across the W1 postcode command an average price of £1.92m compared with the wider Westminster average of £854,198.

Westminster school and Francis Holland school, Sloane Square follow. Both are located within the SW1 postcode, where the average property price stands at £1.49m, a premium of 54.5% compared with Westminster as a whole.

Australian flight transporting aid supplies leaves for Nepal this morning. Follow updates live

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

An RAAF flight containing hygiene kits, shelter, and solar lights will leave for Nepal this morning, as the foreign minister and acting prime minister, Penny Wong, says grave concerns are held over the 43 missing Australians after the Nepal-Tibet flash flood.

More than 4,400 people are still missing on both sides of the border, with more than 930 people confirmed dead. Wong told ABC’s 7.30 program last night that the federal government is urgently seeking to find the whereabouts of the 43 missing Australians.

She said the Australian government has provided $8m in aid so far, and noted that Australian citizens had donated $2m to a public appeal – something that the federal government is matching.

double quotation markWe are deploying an RAAF aircraft to deliver these kits which are designed to support people in circumstances of natural disasters that destroy infrastructure and their shelter.

Whether it’s shelter kits, lights, hygiene kits, these are the things needed for those people who are facing the devastation of their homes and their communities.

On the 43 missing Australians, Wong said Australia has been engaging with the Nepali and Chinese governments but the recovery and search effort is “very difficult”.

Nine of the 43 missing were on the Chinese side of the border at the time of the floods, but no more information was available on the 43 missing, she said.

double quotation markI first want to again express what I’ve been expressing to the families and friends of the 43 Australians who are not accounted for, that this is such a difficult time, it’s an incredibly distressing, traumatic time. I think all Australians are with you. And certainly we are with you. We are working to do whatever we can and to provide any information we obtain.

The typical capital city home price has slipped back below $1m as buyers fail to show up in a “buyers market”, property data firm Cotality has reported.
 The median price in the capitals surpassed $1m for the first time back in October but has steadily fallen this year with demand suppressed by rising interest rates and weak confidence in the economy. By the end of August, it fell to $990,394, Cotality found.

The typical home price in Perth passed $1m in March, but slipped to $999,987 by the end of August.

Sydney and Brisbane are back to being the only capitals with median prices above $1m. Sydney’s is at $1.22m, $93,000 below its peak earlier this year, while Brisbane is at $1.08m, down $30,000 from its peak.

Cotality’s research director, Tim Lawless, said nearly every capital city suburb had now seen prices fall, yet far fewer homes were being sold compared to this time last year, meaning listings on the market were building up. He said:

double quotation markLonger selling times, larger vendor discounting and persistently low auction clearance rates all point to a buyer’s market, yet buyers are lacking the confidence to transact at the moment.

Members of Melbourne’s Nepali and Tibetan communities gathered in the city’s Federation Square last night to remember the victims of the Nepal-Tibet flood.

More than 40 Australians are among thousands of people who remain missing after the natural disaster last week. The overall death toll is at least 810 people.

At the vigil, volunteers unfurled a sign on the ground – encircled by candlelights – that read “Vic united for Nepal”.

The event, organised by the Non-Resident Nepali Association’s Victorian branch, was attended by the Victorian premier, Ben Carroll, and Labor and opposition MPs.

Speaking to the crowd of about 400 people, Carroll said:

double quotation markI know so many of your hearts are breaking right now. Look around you, all of Victoria stands behind you and every candle in Federation Square is lit up for you. You are not alone.

Carroll said the Victoria government had pledged to donate $100,000 to Australia’s immediate efforts in Nepal.

Penny Wong has said Labor accepts there’s a message from WA Labor’s loss to One Nation in the Secret Harbour byelection, but says One Nation leader Pauline Hanson has “very few real solutions”.

Wong told ABC’s 7.30 program the loss was “very disappointing”, but that Labor knows many Australians “believe the status quo is not delivering for them”.

She pointed to policies such a investment in Medicare, childcare, and schools, as well as tax cuts and tax changes as the federal government’s response. Wong accepted that the public had not taken the changes on board in their vote in WA, but said Hanson was not offering solutions.

double quotation markI accept there’s a message sent in this byelection for us. I accept that. And I think we understand that.

We understand the importance of delivering real change and as someone who sits in the Senate with Pauline Hanson, what I would say to you is that she is … there’s a lot of anger and a lot of complaints, but really very few solutions.

articles.title: US Supreme Court clears way for Trump to keep building White House ballroom
articles.excerpt:
Construction continues on a new helipad on the South Lawn of the White House and the East Wing ballroom on 24 August 2026 in Washington DC.

The US Supreme Court has ruled that construction of a $400m...
articles.body_text:
Construction continues on a new helipad on the South Lawn of the White House and the East Wing ballroom on 24 August 2026 in Washington DC.

The US Supreme Court has ruled that construction of a $400m (£297m) ballroom at the White House can go ahead, handing a win to President Donald Trump.

In a 5-4 ruling, the justices granted the Trump administration's emergency request, blocking lower court rulings that would have halted construction of an above-ground portion of the project.

The National Trust for Historic Preservation filed the legal challenge, arguing that the president did not have unilateral authority to proceed with construction.

Trump demolished the historic East Wing of the executive residence last autumn to begin building the ballroom.

On Friday, the high court had temporarily allowed construction of the White House ballroom to move forward.

Chief Justice John Roberts issued a stay, allowing the ballroom project, which includes a military complex, to continue while the high court considered the lawsuit aiming to halt it entirely.

On Monday, it was Roberts, a conservative, who sided with the three dissenting liberal justices to write that "construction is likely unlawful".

The dissenting justices said that Congress "has explicitly prohibited" the construction of any building or structure on federal grounds in the capital "without express authority of Congress".

They added that the legislative branch had "not passed any law resembling 'express authority' for the Executive's construction of it".

In the unsigned order, the five judges who cleared the way for construction said the Trump administration had established that it was likely to succeed in arguing that it would "suffer irreparable harm without a stay, and that the balance of equities tips in its favor".

"Beginning with the merits, the government is likely to prevail in showing that the Trust lacks standing to challenge the East Wing project," they wrote.

Trump has long argued that the White House needs a larger events space, and more recently, that it was important for his security.

The National Trust for Historic Preservation argued that construction was causing irreversible damage to a historical landmark.

A divided US supreme court has permitted Donald Trump to continue building his controversial $400m White House ballroom amid legal challenges.

In a 5-4 ruling, the justices permitted the Trump administration’s request to ⁠block a lower court order which had halted above-ground construction of the project while a lawsuit by a historic preservation group seeks to block it.

The US president, who demolished the historic East Wing of the White House last year to make way for planned ballroom, has repeatedly touted it as “a gift” to the US people.

Monday’s decision from the supreme court comes after a temporary order from Chief Justice John Roberts, which had enabled work to continue.

Roberts opted to dissent from this latest order, however, joining with the court’s three liberal-leaning justices, who described the construction as “likely unlawful”.

articles.body_text:
Vice President JD Vance implored Michigan Democratic Senate nominee to focus on policy issues instead of attacking his wife.

Vice President JD Vance urged Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed during a rally on Monday to focus on substantive policy issues instead of attacking his wife.

"I actually think that the people of Michigan think it's kind of weird when you talk about another guy's wife," Vance said at a metro Detroit rally organized by MAGA Inc., a super PAC aligned with the president.

"I think the people of Michigan would like you to talk about the public policy ideas …I think the people of Michigan would like you to talk about how you're going to protect auto workers when you're supporting every single policy that has undercut the wages and jobs of Michigan auto workers your entire life in public service."

EL-SAYED UNDER FIRE ONLINE AFTER TAKING AIM AT USHA VANCE, FEMALE TRUMP AIDE IN WEEKEND SOCIAL MEDIA POSTS

A split image shows Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed, left, and Vice President JD Vance, right. El-Sayed won the Democratic primary for Michigan's open U.S. Senate seat and will face Republican Mike Rogers in the general election. (Jim Lo Scalzo-Pool/Getty Images; Finn Gomez/Getty Images)

"But whatever you want to talk about, Abdul, keep my wife's name the hell out of your mouth because she's way out of your league," the vice president added.

Vance's quip was in response to El-Sayed saying "do we think JD is taking Usha with him back in time to meet Papaw, or no" after the vice president suggested that Sharia law would have been an alien concept to his grandfather.

Critics said the post appeared to take aim at Usha Vance’s Indian heritage. El-Sayed later said his point was that Vance seemed to be suggesting some people are "more American" than others because their families have been in the country longer, noting that Vance’s own in-laws are immigrants.

"If you’re a rural White American living in Michigan, just remember El-Sayed believes you’re a racist," conservative commentator Ryan Girdusky said in response to the Democratic hopeful’s statement.

SECOND LADY USHA VANCE FIRES BACK AT POINTED JAB FROM DEMOCRATIC SENATE NOMINEE ABDUL EL-SAYED

Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed is facing criticism over recent comments made about VP JD Vance and Second Lady Usha Vance. (Photo by Roberto Schmidt-Pool/Getty Images; Photo by Monica Morgan/Getty Images)

Earlier in his speech, Vance accused El-Sayed of undercutting his support for working people by taking liberal positions on immigration issues.

"We're here to talk about protecting Michigan truck drivers, but also protecting the safety of every single person who drives on the road with a semi truck, which is all of us," Vance said. "Here's the crazy thing. Just a few years ago, Abdul El-Sayed said that we need to make sure that illegal aliens have driver's licenses in this country. He would love to undercut the wages of American truckers."

US Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed speaks during a press conference in Detroit, Mich., on Aug. 5, 2026, after narrowly winning the Michigan Democratic Senate nomination. Fox News Flash top entertainment and celebrity headlines are here.

Carrie Underwood admitted Dolly Parton's death was a shock that created ripples throughout the world.

The "American Idol" judge was overcome with emotion as she honored the late country music icon during her debut performance Saturday at the Tanglewood Music Center in Lenox, Mass.

Underwood, 43, told that audience that Parton was a "huge influence to so many of us, but just one of the nicest people I think I've ever met."

DOLLY PARTON LAID TO REST AS NIECE SHARES EMOTIONAL TRIBUTE TO 'GRANNY'

Carrie Underwood praised Dolly Parton over the weekend during an emotional tribute to the late country legend who died Tuesday, Aug. 26. She was 80. (Mark Selliger)

"It was such a shock, I feel like just to the whole world, like could feel the ripples, like time just stood still, and it was just like ... what?" Underwood said in a video circulating online.

"She's just the one that transcends all space and all time."

DOLLY PARTON'S PATH FROM NASHVILLE NEWCOMER TO BILLBOARD'S NO. 1 COUNTRY MUSIC ARTIST OF ALL TIME

She added, "I feel like she was just out there with the brightest smile on her face up until the very last day ... and that's something that I feel like we can all learn from. She is gone, but she's not forgotten."

The "American Idol" judge noted that Parton's legacy "transcends time" as she praised the "9 to 5" singer. (Terry Wyatt)

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

With one finger pointed up toward the sky, Underwood said, "I know where she is and I know how much she loved Jesus."

The "Jesus Take the Wheel" singer asked the audience to take out their phones and "light this place up" in honor of Dolly before dedicating "See You Again" to the late country legend.

Underwood recognized Parton's longtime devotion to her faith while remembering Dolly on social media following her death.

DOLLY PARTON'S LIFE IN HER OWN WORDS: FROM SMOKY MOUNTAINS POVERTY TO COUNTRY MUSIC IMMORTALITY

"She’s not gone. I know exactly where she is," Underwood wrote on Instagram last week. "She was the epitome of faith, grace, talent, beauty and humor. She had a humble heart for Jesus and made everyone around her feel special.

GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

"She was probably the one person on planet Earth that everyone loved and could agree on. She was a one of one and no one will ever come close. It’s alright to be sad that this world lost a legend, but heaven gained an angel. Well done, good and faithful Dolly. Welcome home."

Parton died peacefully in Nashville, Tenn., on Tuesday following a brief battle with cancer, according to a press release. She was surrounded by loved ones at the Vanderbilt-Ingram Cancer Center.

"Our beloved Dolly Parton spent her life and career bringing joy, laughter, hope and integrity into everything she touched," her team said in a statement.

Dolly Parton's Imagination Library gifted more than 300 million books to children around the world since the country music icon launched the program in 1995. (Courtesy of Dolly Parton's Imagination Library)

"Her unmatched generosity reached the lives of countless people whom she would never meet, yet she was always there to offer a helping hand."

PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

They added, "Whether it be the hundreds of millions of books donated through her invaluable Imagination Library or funding research that helped create a lifesaving vaccine used around the world, Dolly’s unconditional love for all people was the guiding force for her lasting impact."

Beyond music, Parton built a business empire in her home state of Tennessee, with Dollywood becoming one of the state’s most popular attractions. Her charitable work through the Dollywood Foundation and Imagination Library also left an indelible mark on many.

Tracy Wright is an entertainment reporter for Fox News Digital. Send story tips to Tracy.Wright@fox.com.

The Tennessee Volunteers will be honoring Dolly Parton with a helmet sticker this season, the college foot...
articles.body_text:
Beloved singer died last week at the age of 80

Parton was born 30 miles from college campus

The Tennessee Volunteers will be honoring Dolly Parton with a helmet sticker this season, the college football team’s head coach, Josh Heupel, announced on Monday.

Parton, a Tennessee native, died last week at the age of 80 from cancer.

“I’d be remiss if I didn’t also talk about the passing of Dolly Parton,” Heupel said Monday. “All that she’s meant across the world, this country, and certainly, the queen of East Tennessee – a lady that was extremely proud of her roots.”

The singer grew up in Sevierville, roughly 30 miles east of Knoxville, where the University of Tennessee is located.

“You look at [Parton’s] impact, you know, just her ability to give back, make an impact to people, certainly here in East Tennessee. She means a lot to people across this country,” Heupel said. “We’ll be wearing a sticker patch on the back of our helmet to recognize her accomplishments and everything that she’s meant.”

Parton often spoke about her upbringing as one of 12 children in what she described as a “dirt poor” family. Inspired by her youth, Parton led several initiatives to give back to her home town, including her nonprofit Imagination Library, which provides children with access to free books.

The sticker, in the Volunteers’ signature orange, features a butterfly similar to the one in the logo of Dollywood, Parton’s theme park. The logo also has “Dolly” written at its center.

Parton had a close relationship with the university. She twice played on Tennessee’s campus during world tours. In 2023, before a football game, she was walked to the stage at Neyland Stadium by former NFL and Tennessee star Peyton Manning. She then led the crowd in a rendition of Rocky Top, a staple at Volunteers games.

Tennessee host Furman in their season-opener on Saturday.

President Donald Trump meets with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney in the Oval Office at the White House on May 6, 2025, in Washington, D.C. (Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)

articles.title: US health officials exclude measles-related deaths in Pennsylvania from counts
articles.excerpt:
RFK Jr, the health secretary, has suggested the deaths were ‘fabricated’ while the CDC claimed it was reviewing them

Top US health officials and government agencies are currently not including the tw...
articles.body_text:
RFK Jr, the health secretary, has suggested the deaths were ‘fabricated’ while the CDC claimed it was reviewing them

Top US health officials and government agencies are currently not including the two recent measles-associated deaths in Pennsylvania in their counts.

“This is highly unusual,” said Debra Houry, former chief medical officer of the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). She noted that this did not happen with the three deaths reported from measles in Texas and New Mexico last year.

Robert F Kennedy Jr, the secretary of the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), gave the wrong number of measles deaths in a recent interview with Fox News.

“In 10 years, there have been three measles deaths in America,” he said, comparing that with deaths from “food-induced illness” – a category the CDC does not appear to track. “The media and certain demagogue politicians are constantly trying to scare us about infectious disease,” Kennedy said, adding that he was attempting to “redirect attention and resource [sic] to the thing that’s really killing Americans, which are foodborne diseases”.

There were three deaths associated with measles in the US last year, the first deaths from the virus in a decade. But Pennsylvania also reported two measles-related deaths in August, including at least one newborn who died soon after birth.

Kennedy has suggested that these two deaths were “fabricated”.

The CDC has also stopped short of reporting deaths from measles in 2026.

The agency posted a note on Friday saying it was delaying its weekly update, keeping the number at zero. On Sunday, the measles landing page appears to have been updated twice, with the two deaths first reported and then replaced with an asterisk.

The CDC will not include the two deaths reported by Pennsylvania “while CDC reviews additional information regarding the circumstances and causes of death”, an explanatory note reads. The agency added that “available information does not establish whether measles caused or contributed to the deaths or whether the individuals died from other causes while infected with measles”.

This is not how deaths reported by states to the CDC are typically handled. The deaths in Texas and New Mexico last year, for instance, were reported by the two states and included in the CDC’s national tally.

Usually, “states notify CDC of reportable cases on things such as measles. CDC does not review or adjudicate these cases unless a state asked for additional assistance”, Houry said.

The unusual approach will probably affect the agency’s relationship with the states that report to it. “CDC and states usually work collaboratively together,” Houry said. “This will undermine that relationship.”

The CDC has not clarified what information it is seeking about these cases and why this data was not acceptable. The agency is “working to determine what actually occurred”, according to a post on X sent by an HHS spokesperson in response to the Guardian’s inquiries.

“The communication coming from CDC’s official channel on Friday was political and not focused on what should be done during an outbreak,” Houry said.

An Amish couple in Lancaster county interviewed by the Atlantic said their newborn son died immediately after birth. The mother was severely ill with measles and went into labor one month early. The baby was born with a pulse, but was not breathing; paramedics were unable to resuscitate him.

The mother said she was concerned about rising measles cases, but she was unable to get vaccinated because she was pregnant. The US has recently fallen below the threshold to keep measles outbreaks in check, which would protect vulnerable infants, pregnant people and others at particular risk of measles.

The father said he had received a voicemail asking him to get in touch with Kennedy, but he had not responded.

In 2021, Kennedy, then the leader of the anti-vaccine organization Children’s Health Defense, praised the Amish of Lancaster county for not vaccinating their children. Though the Amish do not have any formal religious objection to vaccines, they are frequently disconnected from the healthcare system.

While Kennedy said he was attempting to focus on foodborne illnesses, he did not appear to comment on two deaths from the cyclospora outbreak that sickened more than 17,000 Americans this summer, instead saying only that the outbreak was “under control”. Foodborne illnesses also often fall under the umbrella of infectious disease.

articles.title: New report exposes intact Iranian bunker that may hide regime's ongoing nuclear work
articles.excerpt: President Trump warns that Iran would "absolutely" use a nuclear weapon if obtained. Retired Gen. Jack Keane joins Brian Kilmeade to analyze U.S. economic sanctions and military deterrence in the Midd...
articles.body_text:
President Trump warns that Iran would "absolutely" use a nuclear weapon if obtained. Retired Gen. Jack Keane joins Brian Kilmeade to analyze U.S. economic sanctions and military deterrence in the Middle East.

A new report from a leading think tank has revealed what it says is a partially submerged Iranian uranium facility at the Natanz nuclear compound in Iran.

The revelation of the secretive facility raises new concerns over whether Iran’s nuclear weapons apparatus was destroyed during the two American-Israeli-launched wars against the regime in 2025 and 2026.

The Washington, D.C.-based Institute for Science and International Security (ISIS) announced in late August that it has located an underground Iranian facility that is likely linked to uranium enrichment for the possible use in production of atomic weapons.

EXPERTS ‘DEEPLY’ CONCERNED OVER IRAN’S WORK AT UNDERGROUND NUCLEAR SITE

An illustration showing a list of Iran's nuclear facilities, such as Arak's heavy water nuclear reactor and the Natanz enrichment plant.   (FDD/Fox News)

It wrote that "The facility does not appear to have been targeted in the military actions of either 2025 or 2026. Since the June 2025 war, no vehicle activity has been observed at the facility in available satellite imagery."

According to the institute, "The Institute has identified a separately enclosed, partially below-ground, bunkered building at the Natanz Nuclear Complex that was likely intended to serve as uranium hexafluoride… storage facility to support large-scale uranium enrichment at the Natanz Fuel Enrichment Plant. The bunkered structure was constructed between 2010 and 2017, with the bulk of construction occurring between 2015 and 2017."

It further added that "The lesson for today is that any temporary enrichment ban must include a dismantlement and dissolution of remaining capabilities and must not allow for any type of preparatory activity for the end of a ban."

IRAN NUCLEAR DEAL HINGES ON IAEA ACCESS TO LONG-BLOCKED ATOMIC WEAPON SITES, EXPERTS SAY

FILE - This photo released on Nov. 5, 2019, by the Atomic Energy Organization of Iran shows centrifuge machines in the Natanz uranium enrichment facility in central Iran.  (Atomic Energy Organization of Iran via AP, File)

Uranium is the crucial material to produce atomic weapons. Iran’s regime is vehemently opposed to the Trump administration’s demands that it stop enriching uranium and hand over its already enriched uranium.

According to another report by the Institute for Science and International Security in April," From December 2024 to June 2025, a half-year period, Iran almost doubled its stock of 60% enriched uranium to 440 kilograms. This action dramatically increased suspicion that Iran was moving toward a decision to build nuclear weapons, significantly shortening timelines to be able to create a nuclear arsenal with up to ten nuclear weapons."

The U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran’s vast nuclear weapons facility during Operation Midnight Hammer in June 2025 significantly set back Iran’s ability to produce atomic weapons and enrich uranium.

OBAMA-ERA INSPECTION FLAWS IN IRAN COULD PERSIST AS EXPERTS WARN OF NUCLEAR BLIND SPOTS

Iran's President, Masoud Pezeshkian, said they would rebuild the nuclear facilities targeted by the U.S., and make them stronger in 2025. (Iranian Presidency / Handout/Anadolu via Getty Images)

Jason Brodsky, policy director at United Against Nuclear Iran (UANI), told Fox News Digital that "The report assesses the structure at the Natanz nuclear facility was not targeted during Operations Midnight Hammer and Epic Fury. This raises questions as to why the U.S. and Israel did not target the site. Given that Iran is not allowing IAEA [International Atomic Energy Agency] inspections of bombed facilities, in contravention of its NPT [Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons]obligations, this will require Washington and Jerusalem to rely on their own intelligence estimates as to this bunkered building."

Brodsky added, "If it is still intact and can accommodate this kind of enrichment activity, the site should be destroyed in any future strikes. The allowance of such a facility under the JCPOA [Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action] demonstrates the flaws of the agreement — permitting Iran to retain an industrial scale enrichment program following the sunsets of various provisions — and underscores why zero enrichment in Iran has to continue to be the international demand."

When asked about the facility and if the IAEA plans to inspect it, Fredrik Dahl, a spokesman for the IAEA, told Fox News Digital, that "The building you are referring to is well-known to the Agency as part of the Natanz site that the IAEA regularly inspected prior to mid-2025."

This photo taken on May 15, 2023 shows the logo of the International Atomic Energy Agency IAEA at the IAEA headquarters in Vienna, Austria. TO GO WITH "Interview: IAEA chief expects wider, deeper nuclear cooperation with China." (Liu Xinyu/Xinhua via Getty Images)

Asked about the report, Anna Kelly, a White House spokeswoman, told Fox News Digital that "First, Iran’s nuclear facilities were totally obliterated during Operation Midnight Hammer. Now, Operation Economic Outcast is severing every remaining economic lifeline sustaining the Islamic Republic of Iran. President Trump has been clear that Iran can never possess a nuclear weapon, and America is entering the endgame with the single greatest financial offensive ever mounted against an adversary."

Successive U.S. administrations have repeatedly designated the Islamic Republic of Iran since the 1980s as a leading state-sponsor of terrorism.

U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent’s announcement last week that the U.S. imposed the economic equivalent of the military campaign that defeated Nazi Germany on the Islamic Republic of Iran could set off a series of events leading to the dissolution of the nearly 47-year-old dictatorship in Tehran, according to experts.

Bessent’s declaration of economic warfare — formally designated Operation Economic Outcast — follows President Trump’s commitment to launch an "economic D-Day" against the clerical regime. The comprehensive U.S. economic pressure point campaign also aims to isolate the regime with respect to its efforts to rebuild its nuclear weapons facility.

Benjamin Weinthal reports on Israel, Iran, Syria, Turkey and Europe. You can follow Benjamin on Twitter @BenWeinthal, and email him at benjamin.weinthal@fox.com

articles.title: What to know: US court hearing held for alleged Lockerbie bombmaker
articles.excerpt: A United States judge has scheduled a hearing in Washington, DC, to discuss the case against a former Libyan intelligence official accused of participating in the 1988 Lockerbie bombing, an attack on ...
articles.body_text:
A United States judge has scheduled a hearing in Washington, DC, to discuss the case against a former Libyan intelligence official accused of participating in the 1988 Lockerbie bombing, an attack on a commercial aeroplane that killed everyone on board.

The case concerns Abu Agila Mohammad Mas’ud Kheir Al-Marimi, who reportedly worked for Libya’s external security organisation at the time of the bombing.

Federal prosecutors have accused Mas’ud of delivering the bomb that was later loaded onto Pan Am Flight 103, which exploded over Lockerbie, Scotland, on December 21, 1988.

His trial is expected to be the first held in the US for the Lockerbie bombing. Hundreds of people, many of them Americans, were killed in the explosion.

A court hearing is currently scheduled for Tuesday, but the trial has long been delayed.

Jury selection was set to begin last week. But US District Judge Dabney Friedrich unexpectedly postponed the trial, citing the discovery of new evidence. The delay is designed to give Mas’ud’s defence team time to review the new material.

It is yet another stunning development in a saga that has witnessed countless twists and turns. Here’s what you need to know:

The US has accused Mas’ud of making the bomb that downed a Pan American Airways plane bound for New York City.

Just over half an hour after it took off from London’s Heathrow airport, the flight exploded, killing all 259 people on board, including passengers and crew.

The plane was 9.45km (31,000 feet) over Scotland when the bomb went off, and the wreckage tumbled onto the town of Lockerbie, destroying an entire city block and killing 11 people on the ground.

The death toll included citizens of 21 countries, including 190 Americans and 43 from the United Kingdom. The passengers included 35 students from New York’s Syracuse University who were returning from a semester abroad.

Nearly four decades later, the bombing remains the deadliest “terrorist” attack in UK history.

Judge Friedrich did not specify the nature of the newly discovered evidence.

According to The Associated Press news agency, Mas’ud’s lawyers said federal prosecutors disclosed the new evidence to them days before jury selection was scheduled to begin.

They added that “constitutional and ethical obligations require the defense to investigate this development”.

The possible identity of the Lockerbie bombmaker has remained a mystery for years, but US prosecutors have accused Mas’ud of taking part in making and planting the explosive.

Mas’ud, now in his mid-70s, is charged with two counts of destruction of an aircraft resulting in death. He faces a maximum penalty of life in prison if convicted.

He has denied building the bomb and pleaded not guilty to the charges.

US officials charged Mas’ud on December 21, 2020 – nearly 32 years to the day after the bombing. He was arrested two years later.

According to US prosecutors, Mas’ud worked for the Libyan intelligence service from approximately 1973 to 2011, rising to the rank of colonel.

The US government alleges that Mas’ud and others carried out the bombing at the direction of then-Libyan leader Muammar Gaddafi, who was ousted and killed during the country’s civil war in 2011.

Prosecutors say Mas’ud flew from Libya to Malta with a bomb concealed in a Samsonite suitcase. Upon meeting his co-conspirators, he allegedly set the bomb’s timer to go off 11 hours later.

From there, Mas’ud is accused of handing the bomb to a co-conspirator, who placed the suitcase on an airport conveyor belt, before returning to the Libyan capital, Tripoli.

Two other suspected Libyan intelligence agents, Abd al-Basit al-Magrahi and Al-Amin Khalifa Fahimah, were tried by a panel of Scottish judges in the Netherlands in 2000.

The court acquitted Fahimah and convicted al-Magrahi in 2001, sentencing him to life imprisonment.

Al-Magrahi was released on compassionate grounds in 2009 and died in Libya in 2012. Fahimah died on August 25 this year. US prosecutors believe they met Mas’ud in Malta to plant the bomb.

The Lockerbie bombing has been the subject of a joint Scottish-US investigation since December 1988.

Mas’ud has been in US custody since 2022. He was originally due to stand trial in May 2025.

That date was set aside following a joint request from the prosecution and defence, who cited the complexity of the case and Mas’ud’s ill health.

The trial was scheduled for this past April, but was called off again after Mas’ud’s legal team asked for more time to prepare.

Judge Friedrich has agreed that the trial’s start date should be pushed back. It is now expected that the trial may not start until next year.
